en: The Sāmarahasyopaniṣad:

Once, the sons of Brahmā, Sanaka and the others, desiring to know the ultimate reality, questioned the Grandfather with prostrations: "O Father, we constantly meditate upon those pastimes that occur eternally in Vaikuṇṭha, and we behold them perpetually along with the bliss of consciousness (cidānanda). Please speak if it pleases you. What do they call the Brahman that is the essence of the bliss of consciousness? They call that Brahman which exists pervading the universe through its all-pervasiveness. Does the Puruṣa enter into Prakṛti?"

"Why does there exist a connection with primordial nature (*prakṛti*)? What is the nature of living beings (*jīva*)? From what do they arise? Of what measure are their worlds and non-worlds, as described by those who know the ancient lore? The Grandfather said: "This Dharma was heard from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa. Listen, all of you, to how this creation comes into being. Transcending both the perishable and the imperishable, the world consisting of bliss, known as Puruṣottama and accessible through devotion, shines forth."

The individual souls (*jīvas*) are born from the upward glance (*uttara-kaṭākṣa*) of that Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*); for them, this path of affection (*sneha-mārga*) is attained. Those born from the downward glance (*dakṣiṇa-kaṭākṣa*) are dull-witted by their karma, demonic (*āsura*), and possessors of little devotion. From that side, which is the very nature of Rasikānanda, two forms were manifested. First, Bhaktisundarī was manifested; afterwards, Māyādāsī was manifested. Of these two, the first was his most beloved.

Living beings born from the side of devotion (*bhakti*) follow the path of affection. Those born from *māyā* are demonic (*āsura*), inert due to their ritualistic actions, and devoted only to other doctrines; they become demonic when they find delight in the path of karma. That devotion is indeed threefold. One type is mixed with karma, belonging especially to the gods, the sages, and the practitioners of yoga. It consists of hearing, chanting, remembering, bowing, serving, offering articles of worship, and self-surrender through the mood of servitude (*dāsya-bhāva*).

These living beings belong exclusively to the path of devotion (*bhakti-mārga*). This very same Person (*puruṣa*) has manifested His own essential nature for the sake of His own delight. Those who know the ancient lore call this the essence of nectar (*rasa*), the flavor of bliss from which all flavors of bliss are manifested. This Person delights within those whose forms are bliss. This very same Person Himself became intent upon worship; therefore, He Himself performed the worship. Consequently, in both the world and the Veda, Śrī Rādhā is celebrated.

The creation that emerged from His essential nature was rendered perfectly accessible for the enjoyment of connoisseurs by Rasikānanda. This aesthetic path (*rasātmaka-mārga*) transcends the traditional categories of means of knowledge and objects of knowledge. Those who are devoted to this path find themselves generating within themselves a creation consisting of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). This is the dialogue between Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa: Nārāyaṇa remained in Vaikuṇṭha constantly singing of the secret pastimes with Ramā.

In Vaikuṇṭha, Nārāyaṇa himself, the delighter of Ramā, became absorbed in meditation. Then Lakṣmī, who was worshipping him in private, observed that state of his and, bowing with humility, asked: "What are you meditating upon? What are you chanting? A great curiosity dwells in my mind: who is this deity superior to you, and what world is it, of which you are meditating?"

"Every moment, what kind of play does your mind engage in? He replied to Lakṣmī: "It is the great abode of divine play, superior to both the perishable and the imperishable, the sovereign seat of Puruṣottama. Therein are seven luminous enclosures; therein the cosmic eggs are produced and dissolved; and by the millions, the shells of those eggs are produced and dissolved."

She, Lakṣmī, spoke again: "Aho! Describe in detail the abode of Rasikānanda, who is superior to both the perishable and the imperishable, and from whose majesty Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the other gods, as well as the guardians of the quarters, arise by the millions and dissolve back into him. He replied: "In the beginning, there are the eternally established pastimes of Puruṣottama Rasikānanda. This Person is without beginning and exists as one alone."

Having divided that very form into two, He became intent upon her worship. Therefore, those who know the Vedas call that Rādhā Rasikānanda (the Bliss of the Connoisseurs). Therefore, this world is composed of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Wherever this Person rejoices, there this rasa flows. For this reason, the pastimes of Vraja are sung of in both the world and the Veda. Within that [region], there are twelve forests, each having its own distinct name.

The Tālavana forest, the Bṛhadvana forest, the Kumudavana forest, the Lohavana forest, the Bakulavana forest, the Bhāṇḍīravana forest, the Mahāvana forest, Goṣṭha, the Kāmyavana forest, the ever-auspicious Ariṣṭa, the Dadhivana forest, and Vṛndāvana. Those who know the Vedas call this world eternally full of bliss; therein lies Vṛndāvana, which brings all desires and happiness. Therein the trees are indeed the deities presiding over them (ādhidaivika). Therein are Sādhanavaṭa and Bhāṇḍīravaṭa, and there are Vaśīvaṭa and Saṃketavaṭa.

Where other trees such as the *kadamba* and others flourish; where the Yamunā flows, studded with jewels and bound by banks on both sides; where groves of water-lilies shine; where flocks of swans and cranes abound in beauty, intent upon their play; and where millions of bowers and thickets adorn its banks—in that very region stands this Mount Govardhana. This mountain, composed of jewels, shines resplendently; this mountain is the place of dalliance for Śrī Rādhikā.

This very mountain is always the place of play for Rasikānanda in Vṛndāvana. In that forest, the multitudes of beasts and birds have attained a divine (ādhidaivikī) creation and are always possessed of spiritual experience. That which is the divine creation is the creation within that world.

One attains the state of the world. That creation is of two kinds: one is *saṃsiddhā* (naturally perfected), and the other is *sādhanasiddhā* (perfected through practice). That which is *saṃsiddhā* arises from the very nature of that goddess of the grove (*nikuñjadevī*). That which is *sādhanasiddhā* has entered the path of devotion. Devotees attain that divine play (*līlā*) through that very disposition.

Regarding the accessories for the *rasa-līlā*: in the setting of the *rasa-līlā*, the female friends (*sakhīs*) are endowed with the quality of cleverness; accompanied by their groups of companions, they are full of the perfection of youth, proficient in many arts, and filled with aesthetic emotion (*rasa-bhāva*). There, rows of sandalwood trees shine resplendently. Those trees are entwined with creepers of gems and coral, and blended with gold and fragrance; their flowers are most magnificent. There, the groups of friends stand holding food in their hands.

In those rows, the doors are woven with creepers and endowed with jeweled vines. There, a circle of jewels, consisting of radiant light, shines together with a jeweled pavilion. Hundreds of jeweled pillars, entwined with creepers, are resplendent. Within that pavilion, all around upon the golden walls, the radiant jewels are set and shine brilliantly.

There, upon the plateaus, moonstone gems illuminate water-crystals and streams of water. Filled with that water, fragrant gem-studded lotus-pools shine resplendently. There, fully blossomed lotuses—white, red, and yellow—bestow a captivating beauty. The pollen rising there perfumes that forest. There, millions of pairs of swans sing of the glory of the Goddess of the Grove in the divine language.

There, where bees with full experience sing the glory of the Goddess of the Grove (Nikuñjadevī) in the divine language (Sanskrit), there are ten temples on each side of the lotus pond, situated at its four corners. Upon the walls made of jewels, artificial birds appear as if they were endowed with consciousness. In the midst of these, here and there, trees attain the state of being groves; they shine with exceedingly tender, radiant leaves. Intoxicated by their fragrance, the bees sing the glory of that Śrī Rādhikā.

There, some trees have their branches and sub-branches bent down by flowers; upon those trees are clusters of blossoms that shine in green, yellow, beautiful white, and pure white. Beneath them, the friends Śṛṅgāravatī and the others arrange beds of flowers, using various creepers [to adorn them].

The trees are covered [with creepers] so that they attain the state of groves (*nikuñja*). There, millions of delightful pleasure-grounds studded with jewels shine forth. In those places dwell Lalitā, Viśākhā, Subhagā, Kalāvatī, Manoramā, Candrakalāmohinī, Gatirativilāsinī, Mohinī, Śāstragītajñā, Guṇajñā, Bhogajñā, Bhogapradā, Kāmapradā, Kāmadā, Kelidā, Suratakalākovidā, Saṃbhogasukhadā, Gatatrapā, Niḥśaṅkaratidā, Sutaraṃ suratāntanidritā, and millions of other female companions.

They become resplendent. Ten palaces are filled with various kinds of food and delicacies, wherein there are numerous cooked dishes prepared with ghee and endowed with manifold flavors. In those palaces, the pungent, bitter, astringent, and sweet tastes created by her friend Bhogavatī are complete and become ever-new at every moment.

There, portions of cooked rice, prepared foods, cakes, milk-puddings, and various other cooked delicacies, combined with diverse vegetables and the six flavors, are served by her friend Annapūrṇā; these are enjoyed by that Goddess of the Grove (Nikuñjadevī). Many garments, appropriate for the occasion and beautiful, have been provided by her friend Vastravatī. Ornaments fashioned by her friend Bhūṣaṇabhūṣyā are there for the pleasure of that Goddess of the Grove; in those mansions, there are tens of millions of beds, meals, and articles of adornment.

Therein, other enjoyments such as the erotic and so forth were prepared by Bhogavatī within those palaces for her pleasure. There, there are ten palaces each with four tiers. In those palaces, beds, meals, and ornaments are arranged in manifold ways. In those palaces, groups of female companions are engaged in their respective tasks.

In their midst is the Rāsa-maṇḍala, consisting of splendor and bliss, which was established by her friend named Vṛndā for the sake of Śrī Rādhikā’s happiness. Within those palaces, one friend, Yogamāyā, maintains a state of uniformity among all the friends everywhere. In that place, the sweet-voiced friends cause the seven musical notes to be heard through their melodious singing.

In that Brahmāṇḍa, whatever supernatural powers (siddhis) such as aṇimā exist, they assume the form of her companions and serve Śrī Rādhikā there. Furthermore, the mountains such as Sumeru, Hemādri, and Malaya, as well as the other treasures (nidhis) belonging to the gods, all belong to her.

For the pleasure of the Goddess of the grove (*nikuñjadevī*), they assume the forms of her companions and serve her circle; within that circle, even Śrī assumes the form of a companion, concealing her own identity as she serves. In the eternal pastimes (*nityalīlā*), even the six seasons assume the forms of companions and serve, bestowing various enjoyments upon those who wander through the rows of groves from time to time. The clouds, having taken the forms of various companions, perform the sprinkling of water.

Kāmadeva also, having assumed the form of a female companion, frequents that place; indeed, even day and night, in his own true form, he serves that maṇḍala by day and by night. By his will, sometimes by day, sometimes at night, sometimes in the morning, sometimes in the evening, sometimes at midday, and sometimes at midnight—in various ways—he serves that maṇḍala from time to time.

The various jewels, medicinal herbs, forest plants, and trees that exist upon the earth attain the divine creation and remain there in service. The rivers, taking on the form of treasures (*nidhi*), remain in service to that mandala. Mountains such as Sumeru, Hemādri, and Malaya remain in service to that place. In the form of companions, others dwelling within the cosmic egg illuminate that place here and there with the intense radiance of their jewels.

Whatever material object exists upon the earth, its divine form (ādhidaivika-rūpa) resides right there; therefore, everything arises from that. Those gods who exist within the universe serve their respective abodes in their divine forms; therefore, they all arise within the universe. With their own verses, the Vedas sing the glory of that Nikunja-goddess in that place. The wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadughā), together with their herd, assume their divine forms and serve her.

Having taken up and partaking of flavors such as curd, milk, *takra*, fresh butter (*navanīta*), clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and so forth, they remain there. In that circle of the *rāsa* dance, filled with these and various other qualities, they serve Śrī Rādhikā together with Rasikānanda. Surrounding that *rāsa* circle, twelve radiant locations are beautifully adorned; one of them is the bathing place (*majjanasthāna*).

Where lotus-pools filled with warm water exist, there the friends beginning with Majjanavatī resort to them for the purpose of bathing. There, other lotus-pools are filled with cool water; and there are rows of forest bowers with gem-studded basins containing water born from the moon.

They are enjoyed there; furthermore, other lotus ponds exist, filled with cool water. These ponds are enjoyed by waters produced from moonstones (*candrakānta-maṇi*) and are filled with pearl-creepers and clusters of pearls. Upon the jeweled creepers, birds reflected in the moonlight perform a dance for one another through the bond of their gaze. This is the second station of love (*śṛṅgāra*), which is occupied by the friend Śṛṅgāravatī.

In that place, the friends Raṅgavatī and the others dwell and rejoice. This is the third station of pride (māna), where the friends Mānavatī and the others cultivate their pride. There, Mandāra trees are entwined with fragrant golden creepers; upon those trees, the flowers are suffused with fragrance. The place, covered by various creepers, is permeated with fragrance, enchanting, and radiant with splendor.

It becomes radiant with splendor, endowed with green and yellow hues. The groves of *mandāra* trees are the abode of Śrī Rādhikā. On the bank of the Yamunā, amidst gentle breezes, a single banyan tree shines forth. Around that banyan tree, rows of groves appear resplendent; there are twelve such groves. The movements of the female companions are most subtly woven through the spaces between the creepers.

There, Lalitā and her companions engage in a dialogue of questions and answers with Rasikānanda. There is a movement of the friends through the rows of forest groves. Rasikānanda, who is Puruṣottama himself, performs prostrations. The mistress Manoramā herself becomes overcome by amorous emotion within the bower due to excessive pride. The naturally accomplished companions also become filled with such emotion.

Rasikānanda, intensely greedy for flavors, prostrates before all his friends. Seeing that bliss, the friends, who were deeply immersed [in him], become absorbed in the joy of amorous play. This is the fourth place of enjoyment, where Subhojyā is served by her friend; there, the tastes of food, drink, things to be licked, and things to be sucked possess manifold sweetness.

Rasikānanda partakes, together with Śrī Rādhikā, of the exceedingly hot food-flavors cooked by his friend Annapūrṇā, as if they were freshly prepared at that very moment. Rasikānanda remains in the company of Śrī Rādhikā, fully enjoying the scents of aguru, the essences of oils, the nectars of flowers, and various fragrant juices. There are also other items such as betel-leaf, cloves, camphor, cardamom, nutmeg, areca nut, and coconut.

The goddess of the grove (Nikuñjadevī) is attended by Rāmaṇasā, Sahakāra, Bhadrākṣa, and Ikṣurasa, who serve her with sugar-candy and other sweets made from the juice of ground [fruits]. The companions—Lalitā, Raṅgavatī, Bhogavatī, Premotkaṇṭhā, Suratānandā, and Suratarasakovidā—partake of the divine remnants (prasāda) bestowed by Śrī Rādhikā. Therein lies one place of amorous delight for the connoisseurs of rasa, where Pārijātaka trees are perpetually in bloom and bow down in reverence.

There, it is entwined with fragrant golden creepers; by means of fragrant pearl-creepers, the *pārijātaka* trees attain the state of being interlaced in groves. There, a certain bee acts as a messenger to Rādhikā during her period of pride (*māna*) toward Him, employing the skill of divine speech. That bee is dear to Rasikānanda; through his own cleverness, that bee effects the removal of Śrī Rādhikā’s pride.

That bee, possessing the limitlessness of extreme charm and cleverness, a knower of qualities, is perfected by his very nature and accomplished through spiritual practice. That bee becomes a messenger for Rasikānanda; he constantly acts as an assistant in Śrī Rādhikā’s pastimes of pride (*māna-līlā*). Therefore, he becomes exceedingly dear to Rasikānanda. These bees here convey the essence of music with their enchanting sounds.

There lived a certain parrot, perfected by his spiritual practices, in a mandāra bower situated where Śrī Rādhikā maintains her pride. Having observed the cleverness of that bee and having perceived the grace of that goddess of the bower, the parrot was struck with great wonder. Questioned by the parrot, the bee replied: "O friend, who are you? By what spiritual practice did you attain this form? And how did you obtain the office of messenger for Śrī Rasikānanda and Śrī Rādhikā? The bee said:

"O Śuka, who were you previously? By what means did you attain this place of divine play? Śuka said: "I was formerly a Brāhmaṇa born into a family of devotees of Viṣṇu. With single-minded devotion, my mind was dedicated to Hari. One day, I went to the world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka). There, I saw devotees following the path of exclusive devotion (ananya-mārgīya), and I saw devotees following the path of aesthetic relish (rasa-mārgīya). Through association with them, I experienced the divine pastimes of the forest groves (nikuñja-līlā)."

"There, in Ariṣṭa, I previously heard from one who was eating the clay originating from the Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa Puṣkariṇī that it is a place of constant play. The greatness of this clay is the cause for attaining the Great Pastimes. The bee says: "What [did you hear]?"

"Have you heard of its greatness? Śuka replied: "It was personally saluted by Śrī Rasikānanda. From that place, the friends of Śrī Rādhikā, such as Premavatī and others, were born. Furthermore, it was there that the commencement of the *rāsa-līlā* was performed. At that time, this place was personally saluted and mastered through austerity and meditation by Śrī Rasikānanda himself. Therefore, this place is saluted in both the world and the Vedas. I have experienced the very earth of this place."

Thus, this state was attained. This body was nourished by that clay and became perfected through spiritual practice. "O bee, tell me if you have a desire [to stay]. The bee replied: "I too was formerly a *kāyastha* born in the Gauḍa country. I was a Vaiṣṇava who constantly served Rasikānanda with great intensity of love. By the grace of my guru and through association with holy men on the path of rasa, I heard the narrative which is the very form of the path of rasa."

I have experienced the company of those saintly persons; through the medium of their discourse, the nectar has entered my heart. I have become surrendered to the pastimes of rasa. My engagement in the pastimes of rasa arose preceded by the forgetting of all other duties, and faith was born in the narrative of their service.

For those devotees who follow the path of rasa, the abundance of bliss consists of the excellence of love that has entered the mind through the experience of the paths of association, conversation, glorification, and assembly; one should offer whatever one possesses—be it the body, which is the vessel for the most cherished object, or anything else. Thus, having reached the world of Vraja with the devotees by way of this path of direct experience, I became free from all attachments.

Dwelling in that circle of Vraja, contemplating that divine play in every chamber and every grove, I become absorbed in that very state of being. Together with His devotees, I spend my time—whose duration is unknown—with them in mind and speech, thinking, "From this [the Divine] bodily pleasure and the like are to be received, and from this [the Divine] they are to be given. In this way, my spiritual duty (*dharma*) becomes perfected. Through the perfection of that duty, my body became perfected as a means of realization. Then, such a desire arises in my mind alone.

With this desire, I wander in the form of a bee to sing the glory of that goddess of the grove. Afterwards, being pleased, Rasikānanda granted me whatever form I desired in my mind; he gave me this place of honor, saying, "O parrot, may you remain intent on playing in the forest of Śrī Rādhikā in this very spot. That Vṛndāvana is filled with the abundance of happiness at all times by Śrī Rādhikā.

It is always attended by Rasikānanda; there, the breezes serve him with their cool, gentle, and fragrant nature. In that place lies the lotus pond Amṛtodā. In those ponds, the female companions, exhausted from their play with the ball, perform their ablutions. During the act of bathing, flocks of swans, completely immersed in the exceedingly white waves of water, shine resplendently. Above, a row of birds, served by sweet-voiced cuckoos, approaches.

The groups of her friends, immersed in exceeding bliss, remain singing together the multitude of Her virtues. There above is one temple, a place for amorous love (*śṛṅgāra*); one is a place for various kinds of food and edibles; one is for the company of friends, for sitting together, and for the enjoyment of betel, fragrances, and flavorful essences; and one is a bedchamber endowed with fragrant enjoyments made of jewels. In His divine form, Kāma Himself, having assumed the form of the friends, remains serving [Her].

The Mind-born [God of Love] drinks in the delights of sexual union—the various nuances of the aesthetic flavor of passion, accompanied by the glances, gestures, and expressions of the eyes—along with the capacity for the attainment of the bliss of the passion about to be joined, and the pleasure of that which is about to be united. It is ever-new: the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is ever-new through its constant variations of state; the form is ever-new; the play is ever-new; the speech is ever-new. At every single moment, you alone are the happiness of your friends; every state of being remains ever-new.

The eleven rows [of trees] are the constant dwelling place of spring. The *kiṃśuka*, *vakula*, and mango trees, embraced by beautiful *lavaṅga* creepers, possess an abundance of pollen from their deeply hidden clusters of flowers. The groups of female friends, accompanied by the subtle songs of intoxicated cuckoos and bees, enhance the beauty of their hair-ties and garments which have been intensely dyed. Melodious songs arising from the season of spring are being sung.

In that place, the cowherd girls were always filled with curiosity; they remained there sprinkling saffron, camphor, musk, and aloe-wood paste. All the young maidens, their hands interlaced and adorned with gold, were engaged in sprinkling the essence of musk and camphor upon one another. Some cowherd girls were anointing, some were rubbing, and some were applying collyrium to their eyes, while others sang songs. Those friends adorned the Queen of Vraja, the mistress of Vraja, who was herself resplendent with the beauty of her attire and ornaments.
In that place, the spring season, assuming the form of a female companion, remained attending upon that Queen of Vraja. There—

There, the onset of spring generates a state of passion. That passion, assuming the form of a female friend, remains in attendance. In that state of love, the Queen of Vraja serves that goddess; and by enumerating her manifold virtues, she sometimes serves the Spring comfortably through the influence of flowers, sometimes through the influence of fruits, and sometimes through the influence of tender sprouts. At times, being served by the songs of birds, she extends her service.

In some places, through the openings between the creepers, intoxicated bees, cuckoos, and parrots appear, performing songs. Rasikānanda, having prepared a bed with leaves and sprouts produced by spring along with that goddess of the grove (*nikuñjadevī*), remains there experiencing the pleasures of spring. Among the various creepers, the female companions, adorned with clusters of flowers, fashion beds of diverse kinds in every bower. Through the art of love’s implements, he who knows the play of sexual union experienced the bliss of the fever of passion.

Having attained the bliss of the essence of delight in amorous play, he manifests himself in the form of various arts. There arise the charms of coquetry, emotion, and playful sport. Spring, together with Kāma, expands the delight of aesthetic play. There, many creepers, blooming with flowers born of spring, become bent low in the forest dalliance. Possessed by various curiosities, the female friends, headed by Premavatī, became overcome with intense emotion.

In that pastime, four friends attend upon Śrī Rādhikā. By whom can the bliss of that springtime be described? The four friends have been mentioned; hear their names: Raṅgavatī, Guṇavatī, Gānavatī, and Manoramā. These friends remain serving in that springtime place. That springtime place is exceedingly dear to Śrī Rādhikā.

That place is served by Śrī Rādhikā together with Rasikānanda. There, those friends expand the state of love; Raṅgavatī expands the playful dance of the mellows; and through various emotions, she expands the enjoyments of the spring festival. Thus, she expands the bliss of amorous union characterized by the distinctions of manifold emotions.

Guṇavatī, through the flute-like channel of the lute, scent, and the flavors of the theater of passion, awakens the amorous play of all her companions. Gānavatī, by the quality of her singing, delights Śrī Rādhikā, the joy of the Lord of Rasikas. Manoramā has attained a state of most enchanting emotion.

It comes to pass that those friends, having attained the state of being [the Lord’s] own nature, become perfected through their means of realization (*sādhana*). They said: "What was the means for them, by which that means led to the attainment of Vasantalīlā’s abode? Oh, how auspicious is this discourse on the path of rasa for the sake of the ultimate liberation of those devotees who follow the path of rasa! Only those whose mental activity is directed toward Śrī Rādhikā with a mind that is free from the duties and actions of the path of affection (*sneha-mārga*), and whose very goal and intense devotion lie in Her alone—they indeed attain that pastime."

Therefore, tell me everything regarding the means they employed. Oh, those friends were the daughters of Vaivasvata Manu. Those maidens played incessantly in their father’s house; they became uniform in appearance, uniform in conduct, uniform in life-force, and attained a state of uniformity of spirit. They were devoted to enumerating his many virtues and were deeply affectionate toward their father. Once, Nārada arrived at that king’s palace. Upon seeing Nārada, those maidens prostrated themselves before him.

That wondrous form was seen, adorned with a crown of matted locks, equipped with garments and ornaments, and intent upon playing the lute. With their hands joined in reverence, they all stood and approached him. Those experts in policy questioned him in such a state with humility: "O Blessed One, you wander the world for the benefit of all beings. Noble souls like yourself, devoted to the welfare of the worlds, show compassion to the miserable who have come for refuge."

Thus entreated, Nārada became pleased and said, "O daughters, what is the desire of your hearts? Tell me all of that in detail. Being thus urged by Nārada, the maidens spoke again: "This world of Vraja is celebrated by devotees who have attained the state of being [in love] within their fathers' homes. Describe it in detail; for as soon as it is heard, it bestows the mellows of divine play (*rasa-līlā*). Therefore, describe that place served by Śrī Rādhikā and Rasikānanda."

No desire arises in their minds. If there is compassion, then describe that expansion of the world. Then Nārada, having understood their mental longing, spoke this: "Listen, O friends, to a secret; it must never be spoken. That place is as radiant as ten million suns."

The knowers of antiquity speak of that Brahman which is composed of splendor and devoid of qualities, from which all creatures have arisen; from whom Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the others are born and into whom they dissolve; and that state which the self-knowing wise attain, as well as the devotees who follow the path of rasa. The maidens said: "Tell us the characteristics of those devotees who follow the path of rasa. Nārada said this: "Those who are worshippers of Rasikānanda perform their devotion with the state of being the Self of all (sarvātmabhāva)."

For those devotees who worship with bliss in the *bhajana*, there is no restriction of caste, stage of life, place, or time. Whoever, having abandoned both merit and demerit, serves Śrī Rasikānanda, attains that divine play (*līlā*). In the minds of those who possess this firm resolve, pure love arises. For those who have thus surrendered to the path of aesthetic relish (*rasa-mārga*), neither merit nor demerit causes any obstruction; even when oppressed by sense objects, they are not truly afflicted.

For those who are constantly attached to discourse on service day and night, there arises the bliss of devotion (*bhajanānanda*). Those devotees who have taken refuge in that path—whatever material thing may be given to them or received from them—is to be accepted. The business of devotees is with other devotees, not with others. Among devotees, only a devotee is a kinsman. Family, caste, dharma, and all such things are merely secondary deities. Servants who partake of the divine essence (*rasagāḥ*) have no connection with others.

Aho! [This is achieved] through the Vedas, Purāṇas, Siddhāntas, and Śāstras with their various doctrines; through various rites, vows, fasts, and the like; through restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas); through the established tenets of the Smṛtis composed by various Ṛṣis; through the rules and vows such as fasting on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī); through gifts such as the Tulāpuruṣa; through investigations into the tenets of various philosophical systems (darśanas); through duties appropriate to one's caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama-dharma); through ancestral rites (śrāddha) for the ancestors; and through the determinations of the science of astronomy regarding the times of solar and lunar eclipses, planets, constellations, and stars.

Those whose minds are deluded by the dharmas prescribed in the injunctions and prohibitions of the Smṛtis—those who are bewildered by the rituals of twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), the consecrations of time, the offerings of *bali* and *vaiśvadeva*, the approach to the sacrificial fires, the Vedic path, and other such duties—the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) does not take delight in them. Alas, friends! Those deluded by ritual action never know that divine play (*līlā*). One should never engage in conversation regarding those religious duties with those who maintain the sacred fires, those who observe fire-vows, or those who are inert through ritualism.
Therefore, what is the use of saying more? One should not engage in conversation with, nor touch, those Brāhmaṇas who do not know the path of devotion; one should never speak with them. They said:

"O Blessed One, you wander the world for the welfare of all beings; the virtuous show compassion toward those who have come to them for refuge and are distressed. Therefore, we pray for a vision of that great pastime wherein the Supreme Person, the bliss of the connoisseurs, delights. Thus entreated, the Blessed One showed them that world consisting of supreme bliss. Having been consecrated by the knowledge of the great mantra, those companions became absorbed in the sentiment (*bhāva*) of that pastime. They said:

"Tell me the lore taught by Nārada, by which lore we shall behold the place of the play of Śrī Rasikānanda together with Śrī Rādhikā. He replied: "Listen, O friends! By the immediate practice of this lore, there occurs the touching of the sporting in the Great Forest; by the practice of grace, there occurs the touching of the world of the bliss of amorous play."

One should meditate upon her who grants all desires (*klīṃ*), who bestows enjoyment (*bhrūṃ*), who grants the play of the bliss of the connoisseur (*hrīṃ*), who is skilled in the arts of the pastimes of love (*hrīṃ*), who is the moon of Vṛndāvana (*bāṃ*), whose form is the bliss of sexual union (*sruṃ*), who is captivating (*śrīṃ*), whose body is possessed by the curiosity for play in the forest bowers (*nṛṃ*), who is the essence of enjoyment (*bhrūṃ*), who grants happiness to her friends (*strāṃ*), and who is the soul of the arts of the *rāsa* dance (*hrīṃ*). *Klīṃ*, obeisance! The maidens accepted this lore (*vidyā*) which is the essence of enjoyment, as it was given by Nārada.

For the sake of attaining the bliss of the connoisseurs (*rasika*), one should take up this lore and practice it. In the father’s house of those [maidens], there was a forest exceedingly beautiful and rich with various flowering trees. There, bowers of flowering creepers were most splendid, radiant, and heart-stealing. In that place, those maidens practiced these two lores with the consciousness of Vṛndāvana. Day and night, their thoughts were fixed on Him, their speech was His, their movements were His, and they were absorbed in His essence; immersed in that divine play, they knew nothing else pertaining to the body or the world.

In one place they weep out of thought for Him; in another they dance; in another they speak extraordinary stories; in another they practice spiritual disciplines together with the devotees; and in another, having fashioned the splendor of Vṛndāvana within that forest, they experience the pastimes of Rādhā and Her lover along with His devotees. Once, on the full moon day of the month of Āśvina, during the time of the great festival of the Mahālīlā, the Goddess of the Grove (Nikuñjadevī) granted them a vision. Through an incorporeal voice, She bestowed a boon: "I have known the desire of your hearts. If [you wish] to see My realm..."

A doubt might arise: [He said,] "Having constructed a lotus pond on the summit of Mount Govardhana in Vṛndāvana, you should remain there absorbed in meditation upon Me. By My grace, you shall behold My divine play. Having thus invited them with this boon, He vanished. Those maidens went there and acted accordingly. On that Govardhana, at the Apsarā-puṣkariṇī, they all performed the worship of Śrī Rādhikā according to the previously mentioned method.

Thus devoted, the maidens beheld within a single month that realm—splendid Vṛndāvana, which brings happiness at all times. There, the six seasons serve in their divine forms; there, the grounds are studded with jewels and illuminated by the luster of gems; and there, hundreds of jeweled pillars shine brilliantly with fruits, flowers, and leaves.

Where radiant garlands of jewels are intertwined with coral vines; where pearl necklaces strung upon golden threads are filled with clusters of pearls; where groups of female companions sport with one another in the sentiment of amorous love (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*); where trees, shining with fruits, flowers, and very tender leaves, are densely entwined with creepers; and where the scouts of the female companions appear most beautiful amidst the central rows.

In some places, groves of *bakula* trees were resplendent; in other places, *mandāra* trees shone forth. They were richly adorned with orange trees bearing unfading blossoms. In certain spots, forests of *pārijātaka* trees existed, permeated by fragrant scents. In those groves, intoxicated cuckoos were singing. In some places, the *mandāra* trees, covered with the pollen of flowers, appeared as if draped in garments.

In those rows of trees, those maidens beheld one great place extending twenty-five yojanas. On all sides, there were ponds at each of the four corners, filled with various juices. Ten winds were filled with the essences of filaments, camphor, and musk; ten winds were filled with the essence of agallochum; and ten winds were completely filled with fragrant water.

Ten winds are filled with extremely pure, fragrant warm water; there, ten winds are filled with very cool water mixed with clay. There, in the middle circle—which is twenty-five *yojanas* in length, exceedingly beautiful, and surrounded by the luster of jewels—where the throngs of her female companions sport, there are rows of groves all around, encircled by fine interstices of creepers. In the center of that place is a single jeweled throne, filled with bliss, which is the locus of the joy of amorous play.

In that place, there are these and other female companions who serve that location: she who is full of love, affectionate, virtuous, longing, energetic, possessed of enjoyments, skilled in the arts, musical, charming, blissful in sexual union, imbued with happiness, accompanied by sleep, fearless, free from shame and bashfulness, fortunate, full of erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), and pure in disposition.

Constantly intent on dancing out of curiosity for the sport of *rāsa*, these women—Sugandhā, Kalāvatī, Saṅgītājñā, Aṅgasaṃvalitā, Rāgajñā, and Guṇajñā, as well as others—serve the place of the Siddhānta. There, rows of birds sing together with sweet sounds in various forms. Sometimes they perform the *rāsa* play within the circle of their friends; sometimes they sport upon beds fashioned from flowers and tender leaves within the forest groves.

In some places, they performed amorous pastimes with one another using various flowers upon their limbs and members; in other places, they created the sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) with flower garlands upon their limbs and members; and in some forest bowers, having indulged in the sentiment of love, they remained enjoying great happiness. Upon seeing the lover of Śrī Rādhikā, those maidens were utterly enchanted and offered praises. Exceedingly humble, bowed down with modesty, they paid obeisances and became filled with a spirit of humility.

By that Śrī Rādhikā, her own form was bestowed [upon them], and they were granted fitness for Her great pastimes. Oh, by whom can the majesty of the company of the virtuous (*satsaṅga*) be described? From seeing, touching, conversing, eating together, sleeping together, sitting together, and from the grace of the remnants of the meal, the mercy of Śrī Rādhikā—accompanied by Rasikānanda—comes to pass. Oh, tell me the characteristics of those who worship Rasikānanda, so that I may wander in the company of the virtuous.

Oh, you who possess the great play of sacred learning! Those devotees who, while constantly engaged in service, find themselves beyond the ritual duties of the Vedic path, study the path of Rasikānanda as taught by the Ācārya and become surrendered to that path of the gopīs which was practiced in Vṛndāvana. Oh, those who perform the various duties prescribed by the Smṛtis!

They wander here in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). Those who worship the ancestors (*pitṛs*) attain the world of the ancestors; those who worship the gods through sacrificial rites go to the world of the gods, which they have acquired by their own actions. Those Brahmins who cultivate spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) attain the world of Brahmā. Those who worship the *Gāyatrī* attain dissolution in the solar orb. Among these, one should not even engage in conversation with the Śaivas, the worshippers of Śiva, even by mistake.

If one has engaged in conversation or physical contact with those who are devoted to the *kaivalya* dharma, then one should enter the water along with one's clothes. Alas! If one has engaged in conversation or physical contact with those who worship Rudra and are devoted to the *tamas* dharma, then one should enter the water along with one's clothes. Those who worship Yakṣas should always be avoided. There are numerous varieties of worship for Gaṇapati and Durgā.

If one who worships Rasikānanda should engage in conversation or touch those who follow them, he must enter the water with his clothes on. Those who worship the ritualistic section (Karmakāṇḍa) do not know the path of Rasikānanda; they establish their own doctrines based on the systems of the Jainas, Buddhists, Cārvākas, Mīmāṃsakas, Vedāntins, Naiyāyikas, Pātañjalas, and other such schools. One should not converse with or touch those deluded ones who, being ignorant of the path of devotion, consider themselves learned scholars.

Those Vaiṣṇavas who are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, who are devotees of Nārāyaṇa, and who delight in hearing, chanting, remembering, and saluting Him—those worshippers of the Fish, Tortoise, Boar, Man-lion, Dwarf, Paraśurāma, and Rāma—even they do not know that world. Therefore, their company must be avoided. Even those devotees of Viṣṇu who are endowed with knowledge and dispassion, and who possess exclusive reliance [on Him], do not know that path.

The most subtle path is inaccessible even to Brahmā and others, to Nārada and others, to Rudra and others, and even to the Prajāpatis who are the creators of the world. Therefore, only those favored by that Śrī Rādhikā know that nectar; no others do. When someone worships another deity or harbors hatred toward the Vaiṣṇavas, Puruṣottama Rasikānanda shall not touch them. Oh, listen to the practices of the worshippers of Rasikānanda!

Those who are firmly resolved in their minds and hearts, who worship His pastimes (*līlā*), whose minds are captivated by sacred narratives (*satkathā*), and who through association with those who worship His pastimes become intent on discourse and chanting—those worshippers of the pastimes of Vṛndāvana, through service to Him and absorption in Him, become free from sorrow, delusion, fear, and agitation; they are devoid of envy and egoism, and are endowed with knowledge and detachment. For those immersed in the nectar of His pastimes, that very devotion is their only goal.

Worship of Him alone is the means of accomplishment; those who are devoted to Him alone are one's kin; those who are devoted to Him alone are one's family. Thus one becomes absorbed in the play of aesthetic rasa (*rasalīlā*). Having abandoned the duties of home and so forth, having abandoned the duties of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), having abandoned the duties of birth and family, having abandoned the duties pertaining to liberation (*mokṣadharma*), having abandoned the duties of renunciation (*saṃnyāsadharma*), and having abandoned those duties established by place, time, action, and nature—one should practice the play of rasa.

"Tell me the limit of service for the *rasa-līlā*, by which method the attainment of the Great *Līlā* occurs, and how there may be the vision of its devotees. He replied: "The worship of the *rasa-līlā* is threefold in nature. One is consisting of meditation (*dhyāna*). One should become absorbed in meditation in every grove and at every tree. Day and night, contemplating Rasikānanda together with Śrī Rādhikā within the heart, one should become imbued with the mood of a female companion (*sakhī-bhāva*)."

By the power of that [devotion], one shakes off the male gender and becomes absorbed in the great divine play (*mahālīlā*). Listen now to the second method of worship, by which Rasikānanda may come within the range of one's vision along with Śrī Rādhikā. Having fashioned an image of Rasikānanda—whether made of stone or metal—accompanied by Śrī Rādhikā, he who worships with affection through beddings, meals, amorous pastimes, and royal services, and who practices worship while immersed in that state day and night, [attains Him].

One attains that divine play (*līlā*). For those devotees who worship Rasikānanda, there is the observance of vows for His service. Oh, the service of such devotees is indeed exceedingly difficult to obtain! Śrī Rasikānanda, together with Śrī Rādhikā, becomes pleased with those in whose hearts this resolve has taken root. The service of devotees is, however, extremely rare. Those who follow the path of actionlessness (*niṣkarmamārga*) and have entered solely into the path of devotion (*bhaktimārga*) are truly worthy of service and worship.

Those who, having abandoned other dharmas, are servants of Rasikānanda are the true devotees (bhaktas), and no others. How do devotees become those who serve well? Therefore, by serving well, devotees bestow their grace. Through the grace of the saintly ones (sādhus) who possess equanimity of mind, there occurs the vision of the Great Divine Play (mahālīlā). Therefore, fixing Rasikānanda within one’s heart, one should serve well through association with the saintly, following the path of the secret teachings of Vṛndāvana. Immersed in supreme rasa, such devotees know nothing else.

"O, having heard the description of the great divine play (mahālīlā), we are not yet satiated! Listen, my sons: the pastime of the forest excursion was previously [described] by Nārāyaṇa before Lakṣmī."

It was told then, and having heard it, I shall now describe it: Aho! Even Nārāyaṇa has not seen this place of the Great Līlā, where eight jewels shine resplendently. By the nectar from moonstones (*candrakānta-maṇi*), the trees are served, blooming with flowers and sprouts. The golden basins for the creepers are radiant and filled with water. There, the trees and creepers, illuminated by sunstones (*sūryakānta-maṇi*), become exceedingly beautiful.

The temples, woven with jeweled creepers, shine forth as if composed of light. The trees, entwined by spreading vines, attain the state of groves (*nikuñja*). Within those groves, the various colors of the creepers blaze brilliantly. There, friends such as Śṛṅgāravatī arrange the bedding and requisites. Beautiful birds, with their sweet warbling, seem to sing in harmony with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) of Śrī Rādhikā.

Flocks of cuckoos sing of the amorous pastimes of Śrī Rādhikā in the divine language with enchanting sounds. In its center is a circle of light; those grounds of light, made of gold, shine brilliantly. Upon that ground, eight jewels are situated all around, from which creepers extend, interwoven with golden and pearl vines, and adorned with flowers and tender leaves.

Each temple becomes endowed with every perfected object. In the pleasure-chamber, beds as white as the foam of milk shine resplendently. There, various foods cooked by a friend who is full of other [virtues] become available for Śrī Rādhikā’s meal, ever new at every moment.

There, the fragrant juices prepared by the friend Sugandharasikā—consisting of many fragrant substances such as aguru, sandalwood, kesara, mṛgamada, karpūra, and so forth—are to be enjoyed by Śrī Rādhikā. There, the amorous delights prepared by the friend Śṛṅgāravatī—consisting of various articles joined with garments and ornaments, beautiful and fashioned for the sake of Śrī Rādhikā—are to be well-enjoyed.

The arenas of love fashioned by Raṅgavatī consist of dialogues and the states of the senses and so forth, intended for the enjoyment of Śrī Rādhikā. The various colorful delights of the arena fashioned by Gānavatī—timely and ever-new at every moment—are exquisite feasts for the sake of Śrī Rādhikā. The fragrant arts fashioned by Nṛtyakavī are prepared for the sake of Śrī Rādhikā. Therein...

In the place called Bhogavatī, a companion prepares various enjoyments; the delicious enjoyments—bitter, pungent, sweet, and astringent—become the food of Śrī Rādhikā. A companion named Rativatī produces the pleasure of various amorous sports; the charming delights of the arts of love become manifest. A companion named Suratānandā prepares various arts of sexual union for Śrī Rādhikā. A companion named Manojñā bestows various states of mind.

The friend who bestows happiness arranges various delights for Rasikānanda on behalf of Rādhikā. All those friends perform the rāsa-līlā through the experience of the arts of joyful play. In that central circle, a well-arranged friend at a certain time orchestrates the rāsa-līlā; having fashioned a radiant throne in the center attended by Kāma, she causes Rasikānanda to enter into union with Śrī Rādhikā.

There, these friends all around display their various arts of play: Kalāvatī, Guṇavatī, Puṣpavatī, Aṅgacapalā, Suratakalākovidā, Rasakalābhijñā, Rasabhāvajñā, and Viparītasuratanṛtyakalākovidā—these and other friends, having manifested their respective qualities within that circle, serve Rasikānanda. Accomplished through practice and fully perfected, these friends serve the two of them in many forms.

"As the devotees are, so shall be their happiness and so their state of divine play (līlābhāva). Again they asked: "What is the extent of that great abode? This nectar is fully perfected (saṃsiddha); in what manner is it perfected? What kind of devotees are those who are perfected? What is their form? The crest-jewel of connoisseurs, the Supreme Person whose nature is bliss, enjoyed with Him [the Lord] Her whose form is the bliss of sporting with Śrī Rādhā, in that very form.

The Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), whose nature is eternal bliss, sports together with her who is likewise of the nature of eternal bliss. He will thus cause her to sport by manifesting in the form of the Gopīs. Approaching while sporting in separate forms, the Gopīs—who are about to sport in that state—occupy a single location as if they were sporting separately.

"What is the extent of their abode? What is the nature of those devotees? And what is the beauty of His sporting form as it is being relished by them? He spoke this again: "The secret is exceedingly beautiful. This *rāsa* dance is of six kinds; it is that which occurs during their very *rāsa-līlā*."

The form [of the place] is a secret abode, extending for a hundred *yojanas* during the Great Pastimes (*mahālīlā*), inlaid with rubies, gold from the Jambū river, and fine gold. Its railings were exceedingly beautiful, adorned with sapphires. In its very center, a place of topaz gems shines brilliantly. Approaching that intensely radiant luster of the jewels, the coral creepers of a hundred bower-groves all around, entwined with fragrant golden vines, spread forth a wealth of exquisite fragrance.

The powers of those very jewels shine forth. A flowering tree and creeper approach, bearing fragrant nectar. Perfumed by that fragrance, the companions (sakhīs) become possessed of ecstatic emotion (bhāva); immersed in the bliss of the delight of amorous play, they—such as the devotees Premavatī and others—attain fitness for the divine pastimes (līlā). In the sport of love, the essence of bliss arises; from that, those companions are born. They come within the range of vision as the aesthetic sentiment of the erotic (śṛṅgāra-rasa).

Therefore, born from that bliss of amorous union, these [pastimes] consist of the bliss of the Self. Wherever this rasa, perfectly perfected through the immersion (*svāveśa*) of that Goddess, reaches each house of those cowherd girls, it bestows a corresponding bliss upon them. Through their very immersion in that rasa, the site of the *rāsa* dance—extending for a hundred *yojanas*, resplendent with sapphire set within a mass of ruby gems, and inlaid with gold and hundreds of jewels—is made manifest.

In that place, hundreds of radiant jeweled pillars, having assumed numerous forms through the divine immersion of the Goddess of the Grove (nikuñjadevī) and dividing themselves, enjoy the bliss of their own essential relish. In whatever forms they appear, so too do the forms of Rasikānanda enjoy bliss. Playing in those various forms, those Goddesses of the Grove attain the bliss of the Vraja-līlā by means of the mood of being the Beloved (svāmibhāva). That indeed is the Rāsa.

This bliss of divine play (*ramaṇānanda*) is joined with bliss. Candrāvalī, Candrabhāgā, Suśroṇī, Subhagā, and hundreds of other wives of cowherds are the *ṛks* of the Vedas; these cowherds are the personifications of the Vedas (*vedapuruṣas*). He himself, by means of the bliss of divine play in his own essential nature (*ātmasvarūpa*), united those gopīs with that very bliss. Just as a rope heated by fire appears as fire itself when it is seen, so too this Gokula appears as fire due to its union with Him.

Those gopīs, experiencing that rasa through that state of being, attained the very nature of that Goddess of the Grove (nikuñjadevī). This occurs during two of the rāsa-dances; however, in the third rāsa, they sported individually with each house, in the very form of Rasikānanda himself. He describes their fitness for the manifestation of His own bliss: while experiencing happiness, they were indeed absorbed in the state of the Self (ātmabhāva).

In the fourth [pastime], however, the cowherd girls, such as Candrāvalī and others, experience bliss through the playful distribution of milk products by the Goddess of the Grove (Nikuñjadevī) via Her own possession; and having obtained their desired objects according to Her word, they enjoy mutual pleasure with their appropriate senses and experience that bliss themselves in its very form together with the crest-jewel of connoisseurs (the Lord). The fifth great pastime was manifested by Herself in the house of Vṛṣabhānu.

This very Ānanda, who is the connoisseur of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), manifested her along with himself within the pastimes of Vraja. He alone became the one to be enjoyed in the form of the bliss of amorous union. In that state where the two exist as a pair in the joy of mutual childhood play, there is but a single form. Thus, in that house of Vṛṣabhānu, there are hundreds of places with walls of rubies, and houses resplendent with borders of refined gold.

Lalitā, Viśākhā, Śṛṅgāravatī, and others—these friends have manifested themselves and attained their own essential nature; they experience rasa, which is of the nature of bliss. Furthermore, hundreds of other women have attained the state of gopīs and participate in that divine play (līlā). Whatever state a woman was destined to attain as a gopī, having reached the gateway of that state for the sake of the Rāsa-līlā, He brought her forth.

A gopī, about to be united with Him in His eternal pastimes, partook of the *gopīcandana*—the cosmetic paste from their bodies—and even their remnants found in the lotus pond. That very thing becomes beneficial for devotees; through the manifestation arising from that cosmetic paste, they attained fitness for the great pastimes. Again, they asked a question regarding their doubts.

Aho! At what time was the *rāsa* performed in Dvārakā? Where is the site of that great pastime (*mahālīlā*) where Puruṣottama, the bliss of the connoisseurs (*rasikānanda*), sports? Who are the devotees here? By whose assistance was the site of the great pastime manifested? Listen, O friends! This is the great nectar (*rasa*) of the cowherd girls (*gopīs*). Those devotees who have attained full conviction experience that nectar within the pastimes of Vraja. There are three kinds of *gopīs*: some are the verses of the Vedas (*veda-ṛcaḥ*), and some are the sons of Agni (*agnikumārāḥ*).
Some perfected beings (saṃsiddhas) become manifest together with Śrī Rādhikā. There are eight groups of these perfected beings; their twelve groups are the sons of Brahmā.

There are Agnikumāras (sons of fire). There are twelve groups of Veda-women. They have attained perfection through spiritual practice (*sādhanasiddhāḥ*)—those devotees who, together with Śrī Rādhikā, are worshippers of Rasikānanda. Those who are *saṃsiddhāḥ* (perfected by nature) possess direct experience within her eternal pastimes (*nityalīlā*). Those Agnikumāras, worshipping Rasikānanda together with Śrī Rādhikā within the pastimes of Vraja, attain that very pastime. To those who are of the nature of the Vedas, a great grace has been bestowed through the mood of separation (*viraha-bhāva*).

First there is the attainment of the Great Pastimes (mahālīlā), followed by separation. Those gopīs, longing in separation, know no other happiness. For their sake, the place of the Great Pastimes was manifested for a distance of five yojanas. Desiring to understand the inner sentiments of their hearts, He sent one of His own associates, who is fit for confidential pastimes. During the pastimes at Dvārakā, the Great Pastimes were manifested; that very same associate leads them back to that very place. Rasikānanda reveals His own pastimes to them.

Having heard of that pastime, Rukmiṇī and the other principal queens became filled with longing. When they requested him, Rasikānanda showed them the great pastime. Then Rasikānanda said to those principal queens, "You ladies are not fit for that pastime; these pastimes transcend the worldly and Vedic codes of conduct. Only those female devotees who follow the path of rasa know that pastime. We are princesses—how could we not be fit for that pastime? Thus she spoke many times.

Requested thus, Rasikānanda said, "So be it," and spoke again: "O princesses, if you have a desire to behold the great divine play (*mahālīlā*), then I shall manifest the divine night (*ādhidevikī rātri*) at midnight. There, this divine moon and the divine devotees suitable for the play will appear. You all must come right there. When they were told this, they were all filled with wonder, exclaiming, "Oh! This pastime is truly most marvelous!"

Having arrived there, the friend Suyogā engaged in the *rāsa-līlā*. There, the friend performed the *rāsa-līlā*. There, Rasikānanda Puruṣottama, with his most enchanting form, captivated their minds. All those gopīs, by the power of Śrī Rādhikā’s grace, took delight. There, Rasikānanda manifested a "Brahma-night" (*brahmarātri*). During that night, they all took delight through hundreds of heart's desires.

At the end of their play, the night of Brahmā came to an end. The princesses staying in Dvārakā saw their elders, Ugrasena, Vasudeva, and others, standing at the gate. The elders present there, enchanted by Rasikānanda, also beheld them. Those nights of theirs had passed away while they were absorbed in meditation on the *rāsa-līlā*. Thinking that the night of Brahmā had ended, they all gathered together there at dawn. There they beheld that very spot.

There, jeweled creepers, pearl creepers, and golden creepers—complete with flowers, leaves, and fruits and entwined with jeweled pillars—attained the state of forest groves (*nikuñja*). Embodied supernatural powers (*siddhis*) were seen stationed right there. Kāmadeva was also seen in that very place together with Rati. The *gopīs* residing there, filled with bliss from aesthetic rasa (*rasikānanda*), saw the playful dalliance of those princesses and their pride melted away. Bowing low with humility, they questioned Rasikānanda.

"Aha! Show us the *rāsa-līlā*! Thus entreated by them, Rasikānanda replied: "This time has passed; the night of Brahmā has already gone. I have told you before that you are not fit for the *rāsa-līlā*. Those who are devoted to the path of ritual action prescribed in the Vedas do not know this *līlā* at all. Therefore, you are not suitable for this *līlā*."

Even those women residing in the world of Brahmā, the world of Rudra, the world of Indra, and the world of the Nāgas do not know this *līlā*. There are many other devotees of mine; they too do not know this *līlā*. Therefore, you have become free from pride, and for that reason, you were not granted a vision of them. Having seen these princesses, Rukmiṇī and the others, who were addressed by Rasikānanda, they became delighted and asked their names.

A female companion born of excellent yoga recounted the names of those gopīs: "This one is known by the name Candrāvalī, as well as the famous Candrakalā; then there are Candrānanā, Rohiṇī, Manoramā, Mādhavī, Puṣpagandhā, Suratakalāvatī, Bhogavatī, Haṃsagamanā, Guṇavatī, Gānavatī, Suratakalākovidā, Suvihāravatī, and Nṛtyakalābhijñā. These companions, along with their respective groups, serve that circle [of the Lord]. They honored those principal queens."

They adorned those women with various fragrant unguents, garments, and ornaments. From the water used by them as leftovers and from the mud of their unguents, the pool known as Gopīpuṣkariṇī came into being; the clay produced therein became exceedingly sacred. Through that devotion, those gopīs attained absorption in the Great Divine Play (mahālīlā). Then Lakṣmī, bowing down with humility, questioned Nārāyaṇa.

"From where did those Agnikumāra sages originate? How did they attain this place? By what means did they become perfected? He replied: "In the past, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, was questioned by Sanaka and the others: 'Describe the place of the Great Pastime (Mahālīlā), where Rasikānanda eternally sports together with Śrī Rādhikā. Distressed by that question, Brahmā became absorbed in meditation. In that state of meditative absorption (samādhi), he beheld the Great Pastime."

Upon seeing him, his sense organs became impaired; consequently, semen was discharged from his organs. That semen fell into the fire, and having fallen into the *gārhapatya* hearth, it took on a human form. From that, the men who were born became the Agnikumāras (Fire-Boys). Thereafter, those sages performed austerities upon the peak of Mount Govardhana. From that day forward, these sages have been serving Vraja.

Once, those sages saw a certain maiden upon the peak of Govardhana Hill. She was graced by Śrī Rādhikā and was enchanting in every limb. Seeing her bathing there in the Apsaras Puṣkariṇī, they became bowed down with humility. That maiden replied to them: "O sages, from where have you come? What are you doing? The sages said: "We are the sons of Brahmā; dwelling in this forest, we are desirous of beholding the pastimes of the divine sports in the Great Forest."

Then those Agnikumāra sages said: "O lady, from where have you come, and what business do you attend to? This is a secret. If there is compassion in your heart, then tell us this secret; for the virtuous are always affectionate toward the distressed. To them, who were graced by that goddess, such a nature of extreme kindness naturally arises. She, however, spoke this out of her own compassion: "Oh, in the past, I too was the daughter of the Great King Rudra."

In his house, playing here and there incessantly with songs of Hari’s pastimes, I have found [the essence of] those pastimes within my mind; he is the son of the sage Vibhaṇḍaka, the preceptor, and she is his wife, beautiful in form, known by the name of Sā.

"By constantly meditating upon and experiencing that pastime (*līlā*), one is graced by that Goddess and becomes fit for that very pastime. Then, one attains the future pastime from the present one being described. They said: "What is the mantra? What is the instruction? What is the meditation upon her? Teach us! If you are compassionate, speak! [The Teacher replied: "Listen to this secret. This essence (*rasa*) is never to be spoken of to just anyone. It is not to be told even to those devotees who are indifferent to both merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*)."

One who practices this science of the secret of rasa attains immediate vision [of the deity]. Oṃ klīṃ klīṃ Rādhe, O Enchantress, O Bestower of Desires, O You whose form is the essence of the arts of amorous play, salutations, salutations unto You! This secret is more difficult to attain than anything for all others. Having chanted this one hundred thousand times immediately with a form that enchants the crest-jewel of those who relish the essence of bliss, one should become absorbed in meditation.

That young maiden, adorned with ornaments of refined gold, would listen to it; she was beautified by golden jewelry set with gems upon which the parting of her hair—smeared with fragrant unguents made glossy by the mass of her locks—was marked with sindūra; she shone with jeweled earrings blazing from her gem-studded ear-ornaments, further enhanced by other decorations such as bracelets; her forehead was graced with various streaks of saffron, musk, camphor, and sandalwood, and was further adorned with a tilaka of precious gems and diamonds.

This [beauty], who brings joy to the connoisseurs by deluding them with the creeper-like eyebrows that serve as the bow of Cupid, remains constantly absorbed in meditation, having attained a state of perpetual possession by his arrows. Having attained her, one becomes a conqueror of the universe. Through the compassionate side-glances of her eyes, she bestows fearlessness upon her devotees. The connoisseur of aesthetic delight (rasikānanda) is captivated by the flickering grace of her eyes, which are like those of a wagtail or a fish. Her nose shines exceedingly with splendor. Her two cheeks appear like golden caskets, radiant with light.

The nose, adorned with ornaments, shines; the bimba-like lower lip, set with gems and pearls, possesses the luster of coral; and the row of teeth takes on the form of stars, shining intensely with splendor. With faces radiant as moonlight and necks held in longing, her cheeks, throat, and other features shine most brilliantly. Bracelets, armlets, and hundreds of rings set with emeralds, though full of brilliance, are eclipsed by the beauty of her arms.

The forehead mark, possessing the brilliance of a star, surpasses all splendor. Her two hands shine resplendently, their fingers highlighted by the application of lac-dye, as if they were made of exceedingly fine jewels. Her golden ornaments, shining intensely, are most radiant. Her breasts... [are exceedingly]... (Note: The final word *vakṣojāvati* appears to be a fragment; it likely intends *vakṣojāv ati-*, meaning "her breasts are exceedingly...")

Adorned with musk and agallochum, these two [breasts] alone serve as the abode for the delight of those who relish the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), and they shine resplendently. With their two creeper-like necklaces strung with pearls, they shine like two mountains. In the vicinity of the deep lake of the navel, the beauty of the fresh line of body hair shines like a row of sapphires set in gold. The waist-belt, radiant with tiny bells, attains the splendor of a constellation of stars formed by gold inlaid with gems.

Resplendent with its hips that dwell in a house enchanting all who behold them, rich in good fortune, the abode of the enemy of Śambara, it shines, surrounded by pure garments, adorned with gold and pearls, and graced by the singular delight of passionate lovers. Her thighs, beautiful as the stalks of plantain trees, possess a fearless splendor; the beauty of her lotus-bud feet, appearing as if stained by the dye of red lac, attains a radiant loveliness. This world, shining with the moon-like luster of her toenails, approaches a state of supreme majesty.

Hear further, O friends: the form of Rasikānanda is eternally to be meditated upon by the Goddess of the Grove (Nikuñjadevī). He is pure bliss, consisting of light and nectar, with hands and feet composed of splendor. Endowed with a dark-golden complexion and a forest garland, wearing a crest of peacock feathers, and engaged in dancing and dramatic performance, he shines most intensely—resplendent, radiant, and beautiful, glowing with his own loveliness. This one Supreme Person alone brings the bliss of dalliance among women; thus, aesthetic flavor (rasa) attains its state of supreme majesty.

He becomes resplendent. This single Rasa alone is divided into two forms as Śrī Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. Salutations again and again to Nityānanda. Therefore, when there is a union of Rasa, devotees—whose minds are fully delighted in that Rasa—approach and join Him who shines in the place of the female friend (Sakhī). Those who know the ancient lore say that He is Brahman, consisting of pure light, blazing with the splendor of ten million suns and the radiance of ten million moons. From Him the evolving creation proceeds.

From that which is ever-shining (*saṃrocamāna*) have arisen the creations, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others; by whose power of majesty they are produced and carry out various creations. By whose power of majesty they extend the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the universe]. From that bliss of love (*premānanda*), this world of eternal bliss becomes manifest. Indeed, the divine creation is nothing but the bliss of love itself.

Therefore, the excellence of the abode of Puruṣottama, who is colored by the bliss of love, shines forth there where millions of forest groves exist, filled with various creepers and knots, and where fragrant trees and the like predominate; and where, within the rows of those groves, the throngs of the gopīs' friends dwell exceedingly.

The magnificent articles of play and adornment, approaching with great splendor, shine forth. In various places, separate sites for amorous pastimes (*śṛṅgāra*) are being prepared. The grounds consist of gold and jewels. The six seasons approach, presiding over the trees bearing fruits and flowers of manifold colors. Listen now to how those very devotees, manifesting in divine forms, experience the vision of such pastimes as they enjoy them.

Out of friendship, this world was created by us after leaving our father’s home; in this forest on the mountain, we have fashioned various places of delight for our own experience, including the divine abode of Vṛndāvana, where, in a most lush lotus-pool, Puruṣottama performs eternal play with the Goddess of the Groves (Nikuñjadevī). At the place of assignation, Rasikānanda, joined with Ramaṇānanda, sports there. Ramaṇānanda is the immersion into the Sovereign Lady of one’s own essential nature (svarūpasvāminī).

Rasikānanda, however, is the absorption into the Supreme Person (puruṣāveśa). Those who study this science of divine play (līlā-vidyā) become united with the company of those associated with Vraja through this very association. Therefore, by means of devotion, they should together with My devotees immerse themselves in the narration of that divine play; wherever they may be at night, being attached to the Supreme Person, they should experience self-bliss in His form.

Indeed, by means of that praise, meditation, experience of His pastimes, and worship of His mantra, those sages—practicing that charming pastime and perceiving it through that very state of being—wandered upon the summit of Mount Govardhana, contemplating themselves as being of that same nature. Through the mood of the rasa of divine love (*ratirasa*), trees, creepers, and herbs attained in countless ways an exceeding fitness for bliss. They chanted that mantra at Śrī Rādhā’s lotus-pool and performed meditation upon it.

They realized that [the deity] was of such a nature, consisting of qualities and of a single flavor; they attained a state of exceedingly intense love. Being destined to be united with supersensuous knowledge, they were granted a vision of her own realm by that Goddess of the Grove through the occasion of their amorous play. Due to her extremely deep affection, she shared her own remnants with them as they served her world out of devotion; she then showed them the site of the Great Rāsa dance during the secret pastimes in Vṛndāvana.

Having attained a state of fitness through that vision, they offered supreme praise: "Obeisance to Agni! Obeisance to the bestower of the essence of bliss! To the bliss of love, the giver of delight, and the bliss of amorous union!"

The princes said: Salutations to Śrī Rasikānanda! Salutations to you! Salutations again and again to Rasikānanda! Salutations to her who dwells in the unmanifest, the cause of all manifestation; salutations to the treasure of auspiciousness, salutations to you, salutations again and again! Salutations to her who increases infinite enjoyment, who is the essence of enjoyment, and the witness of enjoyment; salutations to the one whose form is erotic love (śṛṅgāra); salutations to the two whose forms are enjoyment; salutations to you who sport in autumn, who are endowed with bliss!

Salutations to the one who dwells infinitely; salutations to you whose form is nectar (*rasa*). Salutations to the witness of nectar; salutations to the one whose playful arts are hidden. Salutations to the one whose nature is generosity; salutations to the one who wanders in the forest of Vṛndāvana. Salutations to the one who is the witness of that [forest] in a corresponding manner; salutations to the one whose form is subtle (*aṇu*). Salutations to Dharma; salutations to the one who transcends all dharmas. Salutations again and again to the elephant of the god of love (*Kāmadeva*). Salutations to the one who dwells in secret trysts; salutations to the one who bestows the bliss of the play of giving. Salutations to the one whose form is the happiness of enjoyment.

Salutations to the bestower of ultimate bliss. Salutations to Him who transcends all phenomena (*dharma*). Salutations to the source of infinite happiness. Salutations to the beloved of Śrī Rādhikā. Salutations to the one who relishes the nectar of Śrī Rādhā’s lips. *Klīṃ*: salutations to the two who delight in the amorous play within the groves of the forest of desire (*kāmavana*). *Vrāṃ Vrīṃ*: salutations to the two whose form is eternal bliss, united in secret within Vṛndāvana. *Namaḥ Hrīṃ*: salutations to the two born from the creative emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). *Namaḥ Hrāṃ*: salutations to the two who cause the enjoyment of all consciousness to be heard.

Salutations to you both, who are most dear to the bliss of amorous play. Oṃ, salutations to those who bestow eternal joy upon Śrī Vṛndāvana. Oṃ, salutations to those whose bodies are joined in mutual pastimes within the assembly of friends in Vṛndāvana. Oṃ, salutations to those who enjoy the pleasure of mutual amorous passion. Oṃ, salutations to the enjoyer and the enjoyment of the bliss of primordial and beginningless union. Oṃ, salutations to those whose manifestation of forms occurred for the sake of play in the home of Nanda, the son of Vṛṣabhānu. Oṃ, salutations to those whose forms are praised by Lalitā and the other gopīs.
Oṃ, salutations to the two who delight in the pastimes on the Yamunā. Oṃ, salutations to the two who delight in water-sports. Oṃ, salutations to the two who enjoy the boat upon the waves.

Oṃ, obeisances to the two whose forms enjoy the summer season. Oṃ, obeisances to the two whose forms enjoy the spring season. Oṃ, obeisances to the two who, in autumn, take delight in the sport of the *rāsa* dance and bestow all blissful pastimes. To those whose wondrous youthfulness is perfectly matched by their mastery in the arts of love—to them, again and again, obeisances! To those whose inner abodes of mind are overflowing with supreme affection—to them, again and again, obeisances! Obeisances, again and again, to the two whose forms are the cause of all things. Obeisances, again and again, to the two who manifest in every form.

Salutations again and again to those who manifest through devotion and tenderness; salutations again and again to those who are deluded by their own utterly hidden nature; salutations again and again to those who are worthy of the multitude of qualities that bestow the joy of the sprout of the essence of conviction; salutations again and again to those whose multitude of qualities is permeated by the natural spontaneity of conduct and the splendor of the form of exclusive devotion; salutations again and again to those who convey the presence and absence of the multitude of qualities such as beauty of form, conduct, and the savor of aesthetic rasa; salutations again and again to those who possess a singular form on this earth, identical to the very nature of that [Supreme Reality].

Thus praised with hymns, they immediately beheld [the Goddess]. Upon obtaining that vision, they experienced the side-glance of the Goddess of the Grove (Nikuñjadevī), which resembled ten million suns and was as refreshing as ten million moons. Addressing the Goddess of the Grove in her own form, they said, "O, grant us a boon," and thus entreated her for their heart's desire: "May we become the cowherd girls of Vraja; and through my own infusion, may they become blissful in amorous love within the joy of aesthetic rasa."

Those sons of Agni attained the state of being the true essence within the Vraja during the Great Pastime; they entered into the very form of eternal bliss, their abode being hundreds of forest groves (*nikuñja*) and pleasure grounds. Having multiplied themselves into hundreds of thousands through the Goddess Śrī Rādhikā—the mistress of the groves—those sages caused themselves to be relished by that Goddess in that ocean of aesthetic delight (*rasikānanda*). In her absence, a profound reversal occurred; in that pastime, all states of being became mere emotional moods (*bhāva*).

"Listen, Mahālakṣmī! Even those who follow the ways of the forest and are devoid of knowledge and dispassion attain that Līlā. Therefore, having abandoned both dharma and adharma, and having cast aside both sin and merit, those who have received the command of Rasikānandī attain it. This secret must never be spoken. Lakṣmī spoke again: "By what means did those who were always assistants to the Worthy Ones attain the experience of the eternal Līlā? By what practice were they perfected? They were utterly immersed in the Līlā of supreme rasa."

They attained the bliss of beholding that goddess Śrī Rādhikā in Rasikānanda. What was it that they attained by which they became filled with bliss? He spoke this secret answer: "The friends, having arisen, were eternally joined as collaborators in the pastimes of Vraja; just as before, the cowherds were divided into two groups."

Those cowherds who were always companions in the forest pastimes—namely Suśloka, Devaprastha, Varūtha, Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma, Devahāra, Kumuda, Rociṣmat, Drumaṇa, and others—approach Him while shining with splendor. For the sake of their own pastimes, those cowherds were manifested from the bliss of heaven; He bestowed upon them the bliss of divine love. Through that loving worship, they became worthy of beholding the bliss of His amorous play. Only those who possess the perfection of the bliss of love become truly fit to behold the bliss of His amorous pastimes.

May they possess the fitness for the perfection of amorous delight—the pleasure of sight, touch, conversation, play, and passion—and may they extend to others the capacity to behold the bliss of union.
