May they have singular devotion to the service of the Beloved; may their service consist of establishing Him on the bed, providing requisites, praising His qualities and form, delighting in His songs, meditating upon His pastimes, chanting His glories, remembering them, and attaining His own state of being—service performed at the appropriate times. May they fix their minds upon the service of love and upon the narration of the stories of that service.

Oh Lakṣmī! My forms are manifold, my incarnations are manifold; even those who are my partial portions (*aṃśa*), parts (*kalā*), and full manifestations (*āveśa*) do not know this pastime (*līlā*). Other partial portions of yours that have been born likewise do not know this pastime. And others, by the hundreds and thousands, are themselves unable to reach the end of that pastime. Therefore, let there simply be the attainment of the pastimes appropriate for each respective pastime; neither dharma, nor ritual action (*karma*), nor knowledge (*jñāna*), nor ritual action alone [is sufficient]. There is only the recitation of that pastime.

There is only one way to serve Her pastimes: the worship of those devotees who are the crest-jewels of connoisseurs of rasa, the worshippers of Śrī Rādhāśrī, the most enchanting Lord who is the ocean of the digits of bliss from His eternal youthful sports. Even the Vaiṣṇavas who worship Dharma, such as Sanaka and others, or Nārada and others, though they are fit for those pastimes, do not see Me because they do not resort to the pastimes of Vaikuṇṭha. Nor do Jayanta, Kumuda, Jaya, Vijaya, and others see Me; they do not behold My forms or My manifestations that are suitable for the Rāsa-līlā.
Other ritualists did not see that divine play even in their dreams; oh, what the pinnacle of exclusive devotion! Oh, the excellence of my devotees!

This indeed is the supreme limit; the narration of His pastimes is the supreme limit; and conviction in those pastimes is the supreme limit. All other narratives, religious duties, gifts, vows, pilgrimages, and spiritual practices have been cast aside. Even common devotion—cultivated through restraints, observances, breath control, withdrawal of the senses, and the arts—is abandoned. For those who worship His pastimes, the single Vraja-līlā alone is extended before them. Their delight is fixed in the bliss of amorous play (*ratau ramaṇānande*). This is the established essence of rasa. One should not hear of any other pastime from dry disputants.

Those who perform ritual actions and meditations born of karma are "karma-bound" (karmajaḍa) and demonic (āsura); their company must be abandoned by force, for it corrupts the fluctuations of the mind. One should neither speak with nor listen to those whose company one encounters—they are antagonists to Dharma and do not know that Divine Play (līlā). Therefore, those who firmly establish that Dharma are to be served and worshipped; they bestow that Līlā. One should listen to those whose Dharma is non-dual—this is the Dharma of those on the path of aesthetic relish (rasamārgin).

One should not show one’s own beloved object to those living beings who lack taste for it and are dull-witted by their karma, nor should one even let them hear news of that beloved object. For those whose friends have manifested knowledge, there can be no interest in any other knowledge; since they have a taste for nothing else, they would find distaste elsewhere. Thus, delight manifests in what is their own beloved. They forget whatever else is desired. Through the grace of the Guru and the favor bestowed upon those who have surrendered their very being, delight manifests through the relationship of the benefactor and the beneficiary.

Without intense affection, there can be no attainment. He again poses questions regarding the bliss experienced by that Goddess of the Grove (Nikuñjadevī), who has manifested before Nārāyaṇa along with Lakṣmī: "Where is the abode of those perfected by spiritual practices? By what path is that world attained? What is their own delight? And by what Rasikānanda would one attain that Goddess of the Grove? May the herds of cows be ever within the range of that Goddess's vision."

The Person, who is the bliss of the connoisseur, personally and at his own pleasure strokes them with his hand and partakes himself of flavors such as yogurt, milk, and fresh butter. He personally strokes the backs of those calves with his hand. What is the extent of their dwelling place? Are Nanda and the other cowherds, as well as Vṛṣabhānu and the others, perfected through spiritual practice (*sādhana*) or are they eternally perfected (*saṃsiddha*)? As for Yaśodā and the other women who have attained the state of motherhood, are they eternally perfected from beginningless time or perfected through spiritual practice? Of these [women]...

In the home, this Rasikānanda was previously manifested by Śrī Rādhā herself through her perfected emotions; they became possessed of extreme affection. For those who have attained the blissful happiness of the love of worship (*bhajanapremānanda*), the delight of amorous play itself becomes an ultimate festival. How could there not be an exceeding attachment to His form? For those whose delight is in the very nature of bliss, what else remains to be remembered? He said: "Formerly, the eight Vasus were born at the beginning of creation."

It is heard that eight crores of the Vasus, the foremost of the gods, having heard of my world named Vasu and feeling longing upon hearing of that realm, arrived there by their own divine play (*līlā*). Having attained this majesty, they remained intensely absorbed in the forest pastimes. While their minds were exceedingly eager for those pastimes in Vraja, Rādhā was present; seated with me in the perfected grove (*nikuñja*), they attained a state of being through silence.

Having attained the form of Śrī Rādhā, the essence of the bliss of the *rasika*, which is the playful manifestation of the syllable *Oṃ*, they caused their minds to become imbued with that state of being (*bhāva*) and began singing of those pastimes. Those Vasus said: "Oṃ! Salutations again and again to the two who are joined in the amorous play of Śrī Rādhā and Rasikānanda. Salutations again and again to the Soul of eternal sport. Salutations again and again to the Soul of the curiosity of amorous dalliance. Salutations again and again to the Soul of playful curiosity. Salutations again and again to the one who delights in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). Salutations again and again to the Creator who brings about the perfection of play."

Salutations again and again to the one who performs the immediate fulfillment; salutations again and again to Him at the parting of the hair; salutations again and again to the one who enjoys union in love; salutations again and again to the treasure-trove of bliss from various amorous pastimes; salutations again and again to the crest-jewel of the bliss of the connoisseurs; salutations again and again to the soul of the Rāsa dance and the water-sports; salutations again and again to the one who delights in playful diversion; salutations again and again to the soul permeated by the happiness honored by sexual union; salutations again and again to the one longing for amorous dalliance; salutations again and again to the soul of youth.

Salutations again and again to the one whose essence is the enjoyment of rasa; salutations again and again to the one whose face is suffused with the exhaustion of intense play; salutations again and again to the one whose soul is colored by the first union; salutations again and again to the one whose speech consists of the sweet and charming words of amorous dalliance; salutations again and again to the one whose soul is the soft voice from the cheeks; salutations again and again to the one who bestows happiness upon his friends through the erotic passion on a flower-bed in a bower; salutations again and again to the one whose face is suffused with the bliss of embracing, kissing, and sexual union.

Salutations again and again to him who, through the power of the fullness of the bliss of union, brings delight to the connoisseurs; salutations again and again to the giver of the bliss arising from the application of various postures; salutations to the giver of the bliss of the reverse posture.

Salutations again and again to the noble-minded one, the honored crest-jewel of those who have conquered the aesthetic savor (*rasika*). Salutations again and again to the giver of the bliss of the self of erotic love (*śṛṅgāra*), who has brought under his own control the husbands of women who are mastered by the joy of sexual union. Salutations again and again to the one whose self is united with Lalitā, Viśākhā, Kalāvatī, and Śṛṅgāravatī. Salutations again and again to the beholder of enjoyment and the source of enjoyment. Salutations again and again to the self that is the bliss of the most impassioned lover, experiencing the happiness of the separation (*vipralambha*) fostered by sleep.

Salutations again and again to the crown jewel of those who relish the essence of the pleasure of supreme expertise, to the self that partakes in the state of enjoyment. Salutations again and again to the one who fulfills the essence of all play. Salutations again and again to the inner controller within whom the enjoyments of the bliss of love manifest upon this earth. Salutations again and again to the giver of that bliss which is the very form of bliss upon this earth. Salutations again and again to those very things—whether accomplished or unaccomplished, beautiful and fortunate—which fulfill the intense desires of the heart upon this earth.

Thus praised by the Vasus at that time, this Rudra, being exceedingly pleased, bestowed the manifestation of his own bliss. This foremost of the Vasus became Nanda; the woman named Dharā became Yaśodā. Bṛhadvasu, the best [of them], became Vṛṣabhānu together with Kīrtidevī; and Yatrānanda became Rasikānanda together with Nikunjadevī.

Nanda, Upananda, Bhadrāśva, Kṛtavān, Ugrabhaṅga, Udadhisāmantātirociṣmat, Kātyeya, Matyanagharociṣmat, Duṣṇīṣa, Raśmivasu, Sujaya, and hundreds of other Vasus remained there, having accomplished their spiritual goals. Among their wives, Śrī Yaśodā was the most virtuous. Rasikānanda-śiromaṇi, sporting with the Queen of Vṛndāvana, assumed the form of Nanda for one who worshipped Him in His subtle form characterized by a mere fraction of supreme beauty and charm.

Those cowherds and cowherd girls remained as if they shared a single life-force with one another. Those cowherds became one in spirit, one in form, and one in disposition, for whom Puruṣottama was their sole bliss. Other cowherd girls, manifesting various modes of devotion, performed worship within the bliss of devotion; their affection became exceedingly great. That Lakṣmī said this to Nārāyaṇa: "This world is filled with supreme bliss, in which the treasure-house of pure rasa played with a form that enchants the mind."

Wherein that Queen of Vṛndāvana, whose nature is millions of blisses, performed her childhood sports—of what kind were those places? Of what kind were the dwellings? Tell me everything through the manifestation of bliss; the joy of devotion is the happiness of Śrī Rādhā-rasika-mohana himself.

He engaged in play. He spoke to Lakṣmī: "The house of Nanda, the pinnacle of all prosperity and bliss, he made into a palace of jewels, self-luminous by virtue of its divine form. Its walls were made of rubies; its courtyards, resplendent with ramparts of Jāmbūnada gold. Therein, the house of Vṛṣabhānu was situated a *yojana* away from the house of Nanda. From that place, the twelve rows [of houses] consisted of exceedingly light and delicate jewels."

In those rows, there were many places consisting entirely of spreading creepers. With the coral-like shoots of golden *yūthikā* flowers and the sprouts of jeweled *māraṅga* trees, a place for joyful play was fashioned. This is the rendezvous point there: "O Lakṣmī, how can it be described? It extends for four *yojanas*. From the house of Nanda and Vṛṣabhānu, twelve rows shine forth above the meeting place. In those locations, many [women] dressed in various garments of diverse creepers move about."

The *kadamba* creeper, strung with pearl-like clusters and brilliantly illuminated by the luster of its gems, approaches exceedingly; the thousand-fold bower of the *kadamba* vine, intensely permeated with fragrance, comes forth most beautifully and extensively. The *kadamba* trees—green, yellow, black, and white—their perimeters raised by their own pollen, have become exquisitely fragrant. Bees, greedy for that scent, are fully accomplished and perfected through their practice, repeatedly singing the soft and sweet melody of its fame.

Cuckoos, thrushes, and parrots, perfected and accomplished through their own spiritual practice, dwell there, singing with many tender and melodious notes. Swans, peacocks, and other birds, endowed with beauty and grace, appear in great numbers and are most charming. In that place, which is the bliss of connoisseurs and possesses an exceedingly enchanting form, they sport eternally. The home of Vṛṣabhānu, joined by a multitude of ten thousand companions of the Rāsa dance, is the primary site for the eternal pastimes of the Queen of Vṛndāvana.

The city of Vṛṣabhānu is filled with complete bliss, filled with the bliss of divine love, and endowed with a continuous succession of happiness. All prosperities stand at its gates; the eight great supernatural powers (*aṣṭamahāsiddhi*) stand at every door. An abundance of supreme happiness is naturally and perfectly enjoyed there. All those who possess knowledge and virtue—those fortunate ones characterized by the arts of love, desire, sleep, modesty, love, and longing for union—are resplendent in that place.
In the midst of its groves, there are fragrant and cool jewels that are pleasant to enjoy during the summer and other seasons; in some places, there are fragrant *pārijāta* trees.

Some trees were *campaka* trees, perpetually in bloom and shining with ever-tender leaves, fragrant and sweet-smelling. Some trees sat resplendent, endowed with the fragrance and flavor of ripe fruits. Others were entwined with creepers and possessed an exceeding fragrance; bees, lured by the scent of that perfume, sang joyfully. Some gopīs remained immersed there, while other gopīs adorned her with garments and ornaments.

Some gopīs, deeply attached in love, took their meals with Rādhā and Rasikānanda. Some gopīs, having rocked the swing together with them, remained singing. With joy, some gopīs beheld their own respective forms in His picture-gallery day and night without ceasing, and they rejoiced. The gopīs, taking refuge in ecstatic emotion (*bhāva*), performed worship while singing of His childhood pastimes. Being intensely absorbed, they found bliss through the form of loving devotion (*premabhajana*).

Then the cowherds, immersed in the bliss of the Rasika-Ānanda, perform worship with extreme love. Those who are submerged in the worship of love attain that divine play (*līlā*). This rasa, which is the bliss of worshipping the eternal play, is ineffable. Nanda, Yaśodā, Vṛṣabhānu, Satyā, and other devotees experience the bliss of worship eternally and most intensely. Again and again, there arose the excellence of happiness. Thus, the cowherds and cowherdesses attain absorption in Him (*tanmayatā*).

Having attained the state of being mothers toward Him, those gopīs remained engaged solely in worship within the bliss of devotion. By His grace, their homes became abodes of the perfection of primordial happiness, prosperity, and the attainment of blissful joy. Various implements suitable for diverse forms of worship were prepared for His sake. The prosperity and happiness of the cowherds, cowherd girls, and others exist solely for the purpose of His worship; they attain fitness for that very purpose only for the sake of supreme happiness.

Through the absorption (*svāveśa*) of the Goddess of the Grove (*nikuñjadevī*), who possesses infinite perfection of bliss, they attain the joy of the pinnacle of happiness and attain the state of being fit for that bliss. On this earth, in the land of Bhārata, a world consisting of bliss has been manifested by her very self for the sake of the play of her own creation. In that world of Vraja, all the divine pastimes (*līlā*) exist. Those who are cowherds and cowherdesses experience that transcendental divine play in its most perfect form. That Lakṣmī spoke thus.
Tell me here, in this Vraja-maṇḍala, what the various locations are that constitute the secret; for the ground extending twenty-one yojanas is composed entirely of bliss.

To the south of the Yamunā lies a great sacred site extending five *yojanas*, a monastic ground that is exceedingly subtle and permeated by the manifestation of eternal, secret pastimes. Whatever trees, houses, groves, and other monastic sites existed in that place were presided over by deities (*ādhidaivika*). This *Vaṃśīvaṭa* fig tree was Śiva himself; this *Bhaṇḍīravaṭa* was none other than Indra, the lord of the gods; and the birds dwelling there were all perfected masters (*siddhas*) who had attained spiritual realization.

They were seated continuously with those two. Those humans there who were indeed of a divine nature (ādhidaivika-rūpa), being graced by the Mistress of Vṛndāvana, always manifest that pastime through her grace. Whether they know it or not, whoever possesses devotion toward Her in whatever state of mind they may be, they attain that pastime through that very devotion. Even one situated anywhere at all, if they should eat the earth produced from that Vṛndāvana, they alone attain that pastime.

Those who wear around their necks garlands of flowers from the trees growing in that place cast off all worldly duties and attain that divine play (*līlā*). Constantly singing of that play, they have indeed attained that very play. Those who remember Vṛndāvana at every moment attain the highest state of having fulfilled their life's purpose. Having attained the spiritual play within this realm, they sing of and meditate upon that play.

Those who dwell on that ground, attached by affection, have indeed been born from its creation at the very beginning and exist nowhere else. In that Vṛndāvana, this Govardhana mountain extends for five *yojanas*. It possesses three *yojanas* of seven peaks that are unblemished and free from any metallic ores. There, Puruṣottama, the lover of Śrī Rādhā, sports incessantly. Its caves are exceedingly tender, fragrant, and resplendent.

On this Govardhana, Śrī Rādhā-rasika-śiromaṇi himself performs his pastimes. This mountain is exceedingly full of bliss; on this very mountain, in ancient times at the beginning of creation, Rudra performed austerities together with Rudrāṇī. By that austerity, Śiva became auspicious (Śiva). Those who perform their ablutions there in the Rudra-śiva Puṣkariṇī attain those divine pastimes. For those who serve that mountain, there exists fitness for the pastimes even in this very body.
This very Govardhana mountain is where Kāmadughā performed her penance; she is this Govinda-puṣkariṇī.

Those who are immersed in love plunge into that Puṣkariṇī and serve it; from time to time, they experience the fitness for beholding it and the attainment of the bliss of supreme love. It was here that I too performed my penance after creating the Mānasa-sarovara. And by Urvaśī, the Apsarā, penance was performed on that Govardhana mountain out of a desire for various worlds.

This world is endowed with direct experience; wherever there are stones surrounded by the names of Śrī Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, the sovereign Lady of Śrī Vṛndāvana dwells within those very stones. Those devotees who perform circumambulation of her along with [the Lord] composed of bliss attain the fitness to behold Her pastimes. During the great festival of Indra’s defeat, I too shall go to that place for a vision, together with Brahmā and the other gods. It is the playground of the most ardent lover of Śrī Rādhā.

That Lakṣmī spoke again as follows: "On this mountain, at what time was penance performed by Rudra in this secret place? Tell me that sport in detail; my mind is exceedingly restless for that story. Who can ever reach satiety in happiness? By what penance and meditation might that state be attained even more intensely? Oh, I am desirous of hearing about that world; tell it to me in detail."

Having thus taken her, who had surrendered in this manner, into his heart, Nārāyaṇa himself addressed her with a mind overflowing with supreme bliss. He said: "Listen, Lakṣmī, to the majesty of this world! Indeed, I am unable to describe it. For those who experience the sight, conversation, and stories of Śrī Rādhikā Rasikānanda while he is engaged in his pastimes, they immediately attain an abundance of affection for the bliss of union with him in his own form. Truly blessed and fulfilled are they!"

Being devoid of other qualities (*dharma*), they attain delight in the bliss of love; there will be an exceeding attachment. Whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or those born of other castes—those hundreds of various caste distinctions—they all attain it. Neither by social class (*varṇa*) nor by religious duty (*dharma*) do they attain that play (*līlā*), for those whose delight lies in the play attain that very play. With a different disposition, those whose minds are possessed by the Lord (*Īśvara*) attain something else entirely. But with that [true] disposition, they never fail to attain Him alone.

For those who do not have the experience of that divine play (līlā), their manifold spiritual practices would be in vain. Even the wise ones who serve the knowledge of Brahman do not attain that play through the realization of the Self. Therefore, the devotees who are fit to behold that play are, by their very nature, [the essence of] her Śrī-Rādhā.

Through the favor bestowed upon their bodies, they come to possess their own physical forms. By the power of serving the instructions of the learned, their own desired meditations, and sacred discourses, there arises in them an attachment to the narration of those experiences. That attachment, when fully joined, becomes delight in the objects of the senses. This attachment to delight becomes established as a state of being (*bhāva*). Those who are favored by this process of the refinement of delight have attained that divine play (*līlā*). Having abandoned everything else, they become experiencers of that very play.

The possibility of experiencing that [bliss] occurs only when the virtuous show compassion and when love arises. Lakṣmī spoke this again: "You have said that this creation of the residents of Vraja has reached a wonderful place, where this Govardhana stands resplendent. On that Govardhana, penance was performed by Rudra together with Rudrāṇī; having fashioned a lotus pond, he undertook his ascetic practice."

Just as this world was seen, praised, described, and meditated upon in the heart by the radiant Rudra, so too does this very world become visible to all devotees. This most beautiful world, through the immersion in the great cosmic play (*mahālīlā*) of all [the deities], becomes the means for bestowing grace upon those devotees.

"How did Rudra attain the vision [of the Lord]? By what means did Śiva achieve perfection? On Mount Govardhana, for how long and in what form did he perform penance? This manifestation has been seen; please tell me in detail if you are inclined toward compassion. He replied: "Formerly, at the beginning of creation, on one occasion, Śiva went to Vaikuṇṭha with Śivā in order to witness His divine play. There, Rudra beheld many beings composed of various creatures engaged in sport."

Having seen and experienced all the sports I played, my senses remained unsatiated. Standing before me, Rudra was filled with great wonder upon seeing my state of meditation, thinking: "Aha! This is Nārāyaṇa himself, the Supreme Brahman, whom Rudra and others meditate upon; the pastimes of whom residing in Vaikuṇṭha are desired by Rudra and others; whom the Ādityas and other gods illuminate; and whose partial incarnations on earth the gods and sages praise."

He whom Ramā always sports with while meditating upon that Nārāyaṇa; he, having reached whom, the fourfold liberations stand waiting at his gate—that abode is more difficult to attain even for all the gods and others. Who indeed performs the worship of that very Nārāyaṇa? Having attained a state of great wonder, Rudra, with palms joined in reverence, praises Nārāyaṇa. That Rudra said: "Obeisance to the infinite, the great, the Vaikuṇṭha, the possessor of Śrī."

Salutations again and again to you, who are eternally composed of light. Contemplating those manifestations of yours—Nṛsiṃha and others, Rāma and others—who appear in manifold forms as your playful incarnations (*līlā*), I have attained the state of Śiva. I have now reached a state of great wonder. I wander upon this earth in constant meditation upon you. Upon whom do you meditate? If it be your grace, please describe everything.

Thus requested by Śiva, I shall describe the state of that world; listen, my dear son, for I constantly meditate upon that realm where Rasikānanda sports in forest excursions with the Mistress of the Groves (Nikuñjeśvarī). It is a secret place of play, where hundreds of groves shine forth, filled with the delights of blissful amorous pastimes, curiosity, passion, and intoxicating diversion. There, this very mountain Govardhana stands resplendent.

In that world, there are rows of *kadamba* groves, deep caverns, and minerals composed of jewels; there, lotus ponds shine, filled with waters as sweet as nectar; and there lie mines of various gems where objects reflect one another, blended with the supreme form of the splendor of moonlight. Let us meditate upon the deity of that world, the person who relishes the essence of bliss together with Śrī Rādhikā, from whose sidelong glance arise the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the worlds and universes.

Knowledge and ignorance, gods and asuras, repeatedly undergo creation, maintenance, and dissolution; therein millions of cosmic eggs shine resplendently. Those conversant with the ancient lore say that Brahman is exceedingly beautiful there, the abode where the lords of yogis attain dissolution. Listen: if you have the desire to see that world, then go. On the district of Vraja stands Govardhana, the king of mountains.

This mountain is composed of jewels, where Rasikānanda was sporting with the Sovereign Lady of Vṛndāvana. All around, twelve forests suitable for play shine forth, adorned with fragrant creepers and medicinal herbs. The sites for their playful excursions resplend with the nectar-like waters of the Yamunā, where the river flows, its two banks beautifully adorned on both sides.
The waters shine, resplendent with the brilliance of rubies, topazes, moonstones, and sunstones; therein, hundreds of groves of *vānīra* reeds flourish upon the Yamunā.

In this place, which is suffused with the exquisite fragrance of clusters of *jāti*, *yūthikā*, *mallikā*, and *suvarṇayūthikā* flowers, the rows of bees, cuckoos, parrots, cranes, and swans—intoxicated by the pollen they carry—shine brilliantly. With their melodious warbling, they sing most intensely the glory of the Goddess of the Grove (*nikuñjadevī*). This is the site of the amorous pastimes of the Goddess of the Grove, whose play is the *līlā* of Vṛndāvana; by the mere remembrance of it, one’s heart becomes permeated with aesthetic rasa.

Those who at every moment say, "Vṛndāvana! Vṛndāvana! cast off the limitation of the body and experience delight in its divine pastimes. May that [state] also be mine eternally, which is beyond the vision even of Brahmā and the other gods. Those who, even from a distance of a thousand *yojanas*, remember Vṛndāvana and say "Vṛndāvana" at every moment, become truly fit for those pastimes. Wherever a devotee of Vṛndāvana dies, that very place becomes a sacred pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*).

Those who wear around their necks garlands marked with *tulasī* wood originating from Vṛndāvana attain the fulfillment of their life's purpose. Upon that [wood], the creepers dwell with delight; there is exceeding love for them. Those trees which are in Vṛndāvana are perfected beings (*siddhas*) belonging to the material realm (*ādhibhautika*). The creepers, perfected through spiritual practice (*sādhana-siddha*), wander here and there, making play-grounds of medicinal herbs. By that Goddess, the Sovereign of Vṛndāvana (*Vṛndāvaneśvarī*), thirty million hosts of forest-dwellers (*pulinda*) were created.

The hosts of Pulindas cast away upon the saline wasteland the bodily remnants—such as excrement and urine—as well as the phlegm, saliva, and urine produced from the bodies of those residents of Vṛndāvana. For those devotees, there exists only a divine body belonging to the realm of the deities (ādhidaivika), which becomes exceedingly rich in auspicious fortune.

Oh, how can the majesty of Śrī Vṛndāvana be described? Whatever the servants do anywhere for the sake of enjoyment, all that enjoyment is shared by Rasikānanda along with the Goddess of the Forest Groves (Nikuñjadevī). That place is a locus of supreme blissful enjoyment; it is my object of meditation as well. I remain constantly absorbed in meditation upon it. Within that Vṛndāvana, the central abode is my constant object of meditation.

Through meditation on that place, I become a state of bliss through the immersion in bliss; through the meditation on bliss, I attain it. O Śiva, you too, having thoroughly directed yourself toward that state of bliss, approach it; enter into meditation. Enter into meditation on the distinctions of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the erotic sentiment (*rati*), and the divine mood (*bhāva*). He who meditates upon every limb and member of the form of the Mistress of Vṛndāvana together with Rasikānanda—

He himself becomes possessed of the state of mind for play. Again Śiva said: "You have mentioned twelve forests; tell me everything about each of those forests individually. He replied: "Listen, O Śiva, to the description of the forests, hearing which one becomes exceedingly happy in the pastimes of Vraja. Mahāvana is the abode of Nanda; Gokula is the abode of the cows; on the Yamunā is the abode of play; and in Vṛndāvana is the abode of the Lord’s (Svāminī’s) pastimes."

In Kāmavana is the seat of Mahālīlā-saṅketa; in Bṛhadvana is the seat of Vṛṣabhānupura and Nandapura; in Lohavana is the seat of Pulinda; in Tālavana is the seat of Upananda and others; in Dadhigrāma is the seat of curd; on the ridge of Govardhana Hill is the seat of the sale of curd; below Govardhana Hill is the seat of the sport of giving gifts to the line of supplicants; and this Govardhana Hill itself is the seat of the sport of amorous dalliance.

In Ariṣṭa, in Gogaṇa, in Kubjavaṭa, likewise in Vṛndāvana, and on the beautiful Govardhana mountain, creation shall take place through the agency of the Universal Soul. O Śiva, in this place, Śrī Rādhā and Rasikānanda alone always perform their dalliance in embodied form, accompanied by their divine pastimes. Their most wonderful and perfected pastimes are ever-present on Mount Govardhana; therefore, perform penance in this abode of bliss.

That Rudra, together with Rudrāṇī, having constructed a lotus pond there, performed meditation upon that world as he had heard it from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa. Through a certain degree of meditation, he became absorbed in contemplation. For ten thousand years, he practiced austerity for the sake of beholding that world. By means of that meditation, he attained a vision of bliss through the exceedingly enchanting form of the Goddess of the Grove appearing within his field of vision.

He envisioned the bliss of dalliance, accompanied by playful sport, shared with his young wife whose form was like a dense flash of lightning. Agitated by the sight of her beauty, Śiva gazed upon her again and again with his three eyes and offered praise with his five mouths. This Śiva spoke: "Aṃ Aṃ! Salutations, salutations to the Infinite One! Śrīṃ Śrīṃ! Salutations, salutations to you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa! Saṃ Saṃ! Salutations, salutations to the one who delights in union!"

Salutations again and again to the one who sports with two by two in Vṛndāvana; salutations again and again to the one who sports in the *kuñja* groves, *kuṃ kuṃ*; salutations again and again to the one who sports with Lalitā, *laṃ laṃ*; salutations again and again to the one who sports in the pleasure-grove, *krīṃ krīṃ*; *rāṃ rāṃ*.

Salutations again and again to the one who captivates Rādhā’s heart; furthermore, salutations again and again to the one devoted to the continuous play of the *rāsa* dance; salutations again and again to the one who is eternally captivating; salutations again and again to the one for whom pleasure is ever dear; salutations again and again to the one for whom song is ever dear; salutations again and again to the bliss of amorous union; salutations again and again to the one for whom embracing is dear; salutations again and again to the immutable one; salutations again and again to the bestower of the bliss and happiness of dalliance; salutations again and again to the one for whom supreme enjoyment is dear; salutations again and again to the inner self.

Salutations again and again to the one who dwells in supreme delight; salutations again and again to the one of most wonderful conduct; salutations again and again to the one in the form of Bhāradvāja; salutations again and again to Rāma; salutations again and again to the giver of liberation; salutations again and again to the beloved of his devotees; salutations again and again to the bestower of bliss upon his devotees; salutations again and again to the giver of supreme joy; salutations again and again to the one skilled in all arts; salutations again and again to the giver of the happiness of great play; salutations again and again to the one who sports in great divine pastimes.

Salutations again and again to the one marked with a musk tilaka; salutations again and again to the bestower of happiness upon friends such as Śṛṅgāravatī and others; salutations again and again to the giver of liberation; salutations again and again to the one who assumes a body by his own will; salutations again and again to the cause of the destruction of sorrow, delusion, fear, detachment, and suffering; salutations again and again to the inner controller; salutations again and again to the bliss of the connoisseurs of rasa; salutations again and again to the one who delights in the playful arts of mutual rāsa-dance; salutations again and again to the bestower of the joy of *vipralambha* (the pain of separation).

"Salutations, salutations to her who possesses exceeding curiosity! Salutations, salutations to the giver of immeasurable bliss! Having thus praised her, Rudra then became silent, his senses alone remaining; yet he was permeated by that state of being. He became full of longing, free from distress, and composed in mind. Having offered praise, he became absorbed in the bliss of the connoisseur (rasikānanda). Then, the Mistress of Vṛndāvana, pleased by that hymn, invited him to choose a boon with these words: "O you who have been praised with this intentional hymn, pray for a boon."

Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, this sacrificer, my devotee, having been invited by her with a boon, took refuge [in her]. "Aha! If you are pleased with me, then show me the place of play in the world of Vraja. This is the boon desired by me. "That boon shall be yours. By that goddess of the grove (nikuñjadevī), this boon was granted: "I have given you divine vision. With this eye, you shall behold my place of recreation on that Govardhana mountain, where Rudra..."

All the pastimes of Vraja appeared before their eyes. First, Nanda’s residence manifested; though it was already adorned with jeweled walls extending across ten million Vaikuṇṭhas and with pillars of choice gems, Nanda’s house became exceedingly vast—twenty-five yojanas in length and five yojanas in height. It was filled with jeweled pillars and perfectly suited for the playful sports of children, wherein Puruṣottama Rasikānanda performs his eternally perfected pastimes.

That Queen of Vraja herself, assuming a divine form, performs pastimes with that Rasikānanda. Just as the manifest experience of the perfected state belongs to Puruṣottama Rasikānanda, so too this manifest experience of His own absorption is extended by Nanda and Vasudeva. From the house of Nanda to the house of Vṛṣabhānu, a distance of one *yojana* was established. Raṅgavatī and other friends, as well as Premavatī and others, prepared the implements for play near Yaśodā.

Upananda’s daughter, named Viśākhā, is truly cognizant of the emotions of Rasikānanda. From the house of Nanda Vṛṣabhānu, twelve rows of the illustrious crest-jewel of connoisseurs (Rasikaśiromaṇi) reside there. The place of dalliance extends for five yojanas; it is exceedingly delightful, filled with millions of desires, and is very soft, inlaid with Jāmbūnada gold. Hundreds of gems, like fragrant Pārijāta trees, are full of the essence of love-play, rich with mutual scents that serve as their ornaments.

The wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpadruma*) grant the fruits of one's desires. The places for the arts of love shine brilliantly, arranged with an abundance of fruits, flowers, and jeweled creepers in green, yellow, white, and bright hues, and swarming with bees; they are entwined by pairs of coral creepers forming bower-groves. Bedding and furnishings suitable for the intense bliss of amorous play are being prepared. Perched upon the branches, birds of many colors gleam with their beaks and wings.

Those birds, gathered together, sing songs of glory with sweet, melodious sounds. Among those birds, some are accomplished in their means and fully perfected. Having renounced the world completely, they remain intensely engaged in mutual conversation. Their darkness is dispelled by the luster of jewels; thus, they remain exceedingly radiant at night and manifest by their brilliance during the day. In that place, Raṅgavatī and Premavatī sport together with Rasikānanda.
The daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, Lalitā, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Candrakalā, Sumukhī, Subhagā, Bhogavatī, Sugandhāṅgī, Ratimatī, Kāmapūrā, and Kāmadā.

Kāmākṣī, Kalāvatī, Hariṇākṣī, Haṃsagamanā, Śṛṅgāravatī, Dṛṣṭimohanā, Jitakāmā, Vaśakāmā, Kāmavardhinī, Sarvāṅgakāmā, Kāmadṛṣṭi, Kāmakalākovidā, Ratidātrī, Ratisukhasaṃpatpradā, Salajjā, Niḥśaṅkā, Nirlajjā, Atiratibhoktrī, Śrāntā, Sotsāhā, Suratāgamajñā, Vanasthānajñā, Saṅketajñā, Latāvṛkṣajñā, Nikuñjaśreṇiṣu Mārgajñā, Latāparīkṣākovidā, Maṇiparīkṣākovidā, and Atisandhijñā.

She understood conventional signs and flavors; she was skilled in the cries of birds, skilled in the languages of birds, and skilled in matters concerning birds; she knew the locations of conventions and understood the intended meanings of things. She was skilled in the preparation of beds, and knew the tastes of foods to be chewed, drunk, sucked, and licked. She distinguished between various fragrances and flavors, and knew the different types of fragrant garments. She was an expert in ornaments and recognized the appropriate variations for different limbs. She understood the proper times for amorous passion and was skilled in musical rhythm. She knew songs and the distinctions between their aesthetic flavors, as well as the different melodies produced on stringed instruments. She discerned fragrances and understood the qualities of the various flavors of the body.

These friends, who know the various types of fragrant dances, who understand the bliss of perfect abundance, who are experts in the art of singing while manifesting the qualities of the *rāsa* play, and who are eager for the arrival of the *rāsa*, sit in the place of recreation; they provide the joy of words regarding the *rāsa-līlā*. In the rows of forest groves that grant happiness in every bower and sub-bower, various groves shine most brilliantly with rows of coral for the sake of the bliss of perfect abundance for the friends. Within those rows, curtains formed by the rising pollen of flowers come into being.

The places, adorned with ornaments that serve as limbs for those created by Him, beautify themselves; the groups of herds, shining and arranged in suitable order upon exceedingly lofty rows, become resplendent. Groups of female companions, about to enjoy themselves upon these rows, begin their activities. In twelve rows, the separate doors from the house of Śrī Nanda and Śrī Vṛṣabhānu shine forth.

Therein lies a circular pleasure-grove, five *yojanas* in extent, with a central area adorned with clusters of jewels upon a ground of Jāmbūnada gold. It is provided with various sporting grounds where one may enjoy all desires through a divine form. Within that circle, the gates of the rows of dwellings shine with distinct splendor. One row is rich with the fragrance of blue lotus vines; it is exceedingly soft—neither too tender nor hard—and in this most wonderfully fashioned place dwells the friend Vṛndā.

For the sake of serving her [Śrī Kṛṣṇa] and Śrī Rādhikā, a bed has been fashioned there within that jeweled vine-grove; it remains there, exceedingly beautiful. Within that [bed], four rows shine forth. In those rows, four lotus-pools are situated. One lotus-pool remains filled with warm water; one lotus-pool remains filled with fragrant, cool water; and one lotus-pool remains filled with nectar-like water (*amṛta*). Therein is a bathing place of extreme splendor consisting of four ponds, where twelve peaks of jewels shine forth.

From one house, hundreds of fragrant oils, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron essences are brought forth; these essences are filled with the juices of flowers, creepers, leaves, bark, and milk, and have been rendered fragrant. Groups of female companions, intent on the act of bathing, cause [the women] to bathe. Majjanāvatī, who possesses the perfection of pleasure in various water-sports, takes exceeding delight in that bathing. For the sake of the water's excellence, a female companion, possessing exceedingly beautiful waves of water, attends upon her.

There, female and male swans and cranes play one after another; following their intense engagement in the sport of splashing in the water, Agni serves there in his divine form as one who bestows supreme happiness. The sun, in the form of rays of an exceedingly subtle nature, remains serving her. She approaches a temple that is a repository of unguents, filled with cosmetics, which bestows physical bliss and shines with great beauty—a place where the rays of the moon dwell in splendor.

They remain there, attended by those of exceedingly subtle brilliance. There, the women known as *raṅgavatyaḥ* apply various cosmetics to the limbs; these highly pleasant and most beautiful cosmetic applications constitute delightful enjoyments. The third chamber, the House of Passion (*śṛṅgāragṛha*), is magnificent, wherein the doors from one room to another are resplendent. There resides the movement of female companions (*sakhīs*); these companions, who move with great passion and grant pleasure, preside over the erotic sentiment.

First, she displays the blossoms of the *mandāra* and *pārijāta* trees, beautifully concealed within her hair-tress perfumed with agallochum; at that moment, her mass of hair, braided into a circular coil, shines resplendently. The Mistress of Vṛndāvana becomes delighted by the exceedingly subtle sound of tiny bells. Her parting (*sīmanta*) is indeed inlaid with gold from Jambūnada, strung with various jewels and pearls. Like clusters of stars upon a cloud illuminated by the moonlight, the flowers, gold, and jewels set in pearls shine forth.

Inlaid with the inner radiance of moonlight, they remain resplendent; with the moonlight intricately entwined within them, she remains like a moon variegated by the shadows of clouds. The pair of earrings possesses a circle of light from the brilliance of the moonstones in the ear-ornaments. The forehead shines exceedingly, intricately woven with the moonlight of the golden and diamond *tilaka* mark. The two jewel-adorned eyebrows shine forth like the two curved bows of the victorious God of Love. Her eyes have surpassed the cleverness of the variegated *khañjana* bird and the fish.

The nose, adorned with gold and pearls, shines most brilliantly; the radiance of the blue, yellow, and red gems of the nose-ornament approaches the nose as it gleams. Her two lips, surpassing the bimba fruit in beauty, were colored like coral. Her face-disk, its chin reddened by the moonlight of pearls set in a diamond necklace, stands like the lunar orb marked with its spot. Her jar-like breasts, encircled by a string of delicate pearls, appear as if covered in flower pollen due to the radiance of the golden gems.

The emerald moonlight from the bracelets upon her vine-like arms causes the splendors of the gems set in her finger-rings to shine forth. Within the hollow of the lake of her navel, the world itself seems to be apprehended. The tiny bells of her waist-belt serve as ornaments for the drum of the god of love. Even the trunks of the lordly elephants are utterly surpassed by her skin in its roughness; as for the plantain trunks, they were excluded from being metaphors for her thighs due to their extreme coolness.

Her lotus-feet were resplendent with two anklets; her bright toes, reaching toward them, became beautiful as they approached. Her gait was exceedingly graceful. Her friend Raṅgavatī stood in a bower among the rows of cane thickets, displaying the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) of Rasikānanda. She shone with a pearl necklace illuminated by dark gold borders, forest garlands, and peacock feathers. Rich with the beauty of limbs variegated by the attire of a dancer adorned with minerals and coral, she drew near.

The two earrings, shaped like sea-monsters (makara), made his face shine with splendor. His golden-yellow garment, adorned with a forest garland and resonant with the sweet sounds produced by the playing of the flute, was radiant. In that central space, there were four rows of paths interwoven with coral creepers and clove vines; a path for circumambulation was formed by these vines entwined around the tops of the trees. In the middle of that row, a single bed-chamber constructed of jeweled bowers shone forth, its moonlight blended and reflected through the crystal-like *puṣparāga* gems inlaid within it.

The jewels shine most brilliantly. Raṅgavatī and Premavatī, with all their ornaments of adornment, bring Nanda’s house to the delight of the connoisseurs through supreme love. Immersed in extreme bliss, other forests are blossoming with the essence of joy; millions have attained perfection. Millions of groups of friends sing songs. Within those rows, paths for the friends to walk back and forth are laid out. On the path, the circles of light illuminated by the jewels shine resplendently.

The fifth terrace is in full bloom, fashioned with various colors; flowers and fruits abound upon its creepers. Many creeper-vines of excellent jewels, with blossoms like moonlight, remain a deep rosy-red. The pathways, where the moonlight of flowering trees and fragrant jewel-creepers intermingle, shine resplendently. The trees, laden with the fruit of nectar, possess various moonlights rippling in waves of intense yellow and red, appearing exceedingly beautiful to one another.

There are exceedingly sweet and delicious fruits hanging down from them; beneath them lie delicate flower-creepers dyed in various colors. Below those creepers are prepared couches for the sake of enjoying the bliss of amorous delight, composed of fragrant flower-sand, provided with suitable and diverse coverings, and truly nourishing the essence of desire. In those rows, many variegated halls shine forth in great splendor.

In those halls, the chambers of subtle, fragrant jewels shine brilliantly. Within them, various kinds of foods—both hard and soft—appear exceedingly beautiful and resplendent. To one side lies a secluded couch where the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu and Suratananda converse. In that pleasure-pavilion, the sixth row is most radiant, adorned with the finest jewels.

The gateway, however, possesses a door-panel set with reddish gems, shining with rows of jewels inlaid in gold. There, the six seasons reside together and serve it most intensely. Where this season of summer prevails, there are lotus-pools of cool water, and on the banks are jeweled pavilions and water-machines made of *candrakānta* gems. There, flocks of female swans sport, while other birds remain experiencing mutual happiness through the celestial language (*devavāṇī*).

Objects of enjoyment such as betel leaves and other luxuries reside in abundance in that place. To the north, there are one hundred temples arranged in a single row, possessing supreme splendor, extending from the seventh door of the *śreṇi*. To the south, one hundred temples likewise shine in a single row, where the groups of friends have their respective places and pleasure gardens are situated. There, Lalitā, Viśākhā, and hundreds of other friends—devotees worthy of the bliss of dalliance—reside in that abode of the joy of amorous love.

In that realm, in every single house, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) dwell in embodied form, resplendent and adorned in manifold ornaments; there, the cowherd girls (gopīs) sport within those homes. There are various flavors, including the essence of fresh butter, tastes cherished by Rādhā, and many varieties of flavors that grant the bliss of tasting. There are numerous enjoyments consisting of the froth of milk, providing pleasant enjoyment. Within them, hundreds of beds, furnished with coverlets, shine brilliantly.

In those places, the female companions, immersed in the bliss of amorous play and the joy of love, gather together the essence of those various implements. This is the eighth section: mangoes, kadamba, plantains, campakas, aśokas, punnāgas, rodhras, mandāras, pārijātas, kalpakas, nīpas, nīras, vaṭas, nyagrodhas, udumbaras, jambūs, saralas, śiṃśupās, aravādīras, vakulas, pippalas, śleṣmātakas, badarīs, tālas, tālīs, forests of sweet branches, cloves, cardamom, jasmine, cinnamon, betel nuts, coconuts, citrons, areca nuts, and many kinds of thorny trees.

In that Kadamba forest during spring, there are *ketakī* plants entwined with flowering creepers, vines entwined with nectar-bearing *amṛtavallī* plants and clusters of many flowers, and climbing plants entwined with the sprouts of *vāsantī*. These are suited for the season, crowded with the essence of abundant watering, and entwined with many creepers; rows of golden basins are arranged like water-lotus ponds filled with deep water. A stream of water emerges from the mouths of water-machines, fashioned with golden jars bound by silk cords.

In the center of that lotus pond, there is a place inlaid with jewels and pearls, pervaded by sprays from water-machines at the gates. The ninth terrace is being sprinkled with water and is prepared with various implements for water-sports. Here and there, solar and lunar lineages of lotuses shine resplendently. In its central area, within a grove of reeds, the Yamunā flows with surging waves, its two banks radiant and bound with jewels.

In that place where the branches of the trees become coral creepers on swings through contact with the water, there the Queen of Vṛndāvana comes upon a swing together with Rasikānanda, while her friends, headed by Lalitā, sing along.

There, peacocks, cuckoos, swans, cranes, and other birds are found singing together, exceedingly intent upon enumerating the multitude of virtues. The tenth terrace is the site for the game of ball-play for Rasikānanda; it is one *yojana* in length, inlaid and set with gold, encrusted with rows of rubies, fashioned from the earth, and resplendent with tiered galleries, shining most brilliantly. In that extremely secluded place is the spot where the game of ball-play is beautifully performed.

All those friends, in their play with the ball, do not overstep the mutual boundaries established for the game of ball-play. Śyāmā, Rasavatī, Lalitā, Śṛṅgāravatī, Raṅgavatī, Kalāvatī, Guṇavatī, Gānavatī, Kuñjavatī, Suśroṇī, Candramukhī, and Candralekhā—all these friends take up the staff for the ball-game and play without transgressing their respective limits. Rasikānanda-Śiromaṇi himself takes up the staff for the ball and plays.

Viśākhā, Candralekhā, Anurādhā—who possesses supreme knowledge of love—who knows the bliss of dalliance, who is instructed in the art of amorous play, who is skilled in the arts of lovemaking, and Gānavatī—all these friends take up the ball-stick and carry the ball without overstepping Śrī Rādhikā’s boundary; in this way, they each carry the ball for one another according to their respective limits.

When Rasikānanda enjoys play with Śrī Rādhikā under the pretext of a ball game, all those friends utter shouts of "Victory! Other friends, such as Puṣpavatī and others, shower flowers. In that place of play, there is a temple beautifully constructed by Premavatī, filled with every luxury and enchanting. Premavatī, preceded by prostrations, leads Rasikānanda along with Śrī Rādhikā to dispel His fatigue.

There, Bhogavatī stands before her, having taken all the articles of enjoyment. There, a well-prepared maidservant, having arranged a beautiful bed endowed with every luxury, leads Rasikānanda along with Śrī Rādhikā while bowing with humility. There, she encourages him in her heart with enthusiasm. There in private, four friends serve him most devotedly; they are full of desire, free from shame, overflowing with passion, and devoted to amorous play as they serve him. Other friends, such as Lalitā and others, beholding that bliss, become immersed in supreme rasa and sing of those pastimes.

Then, at the conclusion of the play, four friends attend upon her; languid with sleep, their eyes half-closed, exceedingly happy, and free from shame, they serve her well. Among them, those born there—Sulajjā, Bhogavatī, and Gānavatī—serve her excellently. Thus, at every opportunity, Rasikānanda enjoys the pleasure of the ball-play together with Śrī Rādhikā. There, the summer season is served by thousands of forest groves.

The lotus ponds, inlaid with jewels, become filled with fragrant, excellent waters. There, the trees bow down, surrounded and laden with flowers and fruits. There, Rasikānanda performs water-sports together with Śrī Rādhikā.

There, Majjanavatī, Taraṅgiṇī, Jalakallolā, Preṅkhitavatī, Sevyamānā, Agādhajalā, Naukāvatī, Suplavanavatī, Jalābhijñā, Sulaharī, and Hastapallavā—these and other friends perform water-sports together with Śrī Rādhikā. There, under the pretext of water-sports, Rasikānanda bestows manifold pleasures. At the conclusion of the water-sports there, the friend Śṛṅgāravatī leads her to a place of adornment; there, Puṣpavatī arranges floral ornaments.

Thus, Śrī Rādhikā, the delight of the connoisseurs, remains engaged in the pastimes of summer together with various companions. Following that, the experience of the monsoon pastimes is described: the monsoon, consisting of the essence of bliss, spreads forth through thousands of forest groves. The clouds, assuming various forms, drench the jeweled ground with water, making it beautiful with lush green grass.

Peacocks, cuckoos, swans, and cranes, accompanied by various birds, frequent the interior of the groves with their diverse sweet notes. The enthusiastic female companions, resplendent in saffron-dyed garments that flash like lightning, serve the bliss of the connoisseur together with Śrī Rādhikā. Various trees, entwined with creepers, bow down under the weight of their flowers. There, Rasikānanda enjoys the happiness of the bliss of amorous union with Śrī Rādhikā through various guises and experiences of love.

Having observed the pastimes of the rainy season, Lalitā and the others come to sing of those very pastimes together. Thereafter, the bliss of the autumnal pastimes is described: autumn spreads forth with thousands of forest groves, shining brilliantly, wherein all the creepers are in full bloom, all the trees are in full bloom, and the minds of all the friends [are delighted].

They are in full bloom. Where the autumnal groves are in full bloom, there in the center is the eternal Rāsa-maṇḍala, always served by Rasikānanda. There, Śrī Rādhikā performs her eternal blissful pastimes together with Her friends. That maṇḍala is five yojanas in extent, adorned with hundreds of pillars made of various colored jewels, covered on all sides by various flowering creepers, and surrounded by twelve rows [of pavilions].

In those rows, many friends appear resplendent. In the first row, friends such as Lalitā and Viśākhā prepare various kinds of articles. In the second row, friends such as Premavatī shine forth. In the third row, friends such as Śṛṅgāravatī perform numerous acts of amorous grace (*śṛṅgāra*), consisting of various ornaments and beautiful forms.

In the fourth row, friends such as Bhogavatī and others prepare various objects of enjoyment and aesthetic delights. In the fifth row, friends such as Puṣpavatī and others fashion various and wonderful garlands. In the sixth row, friends such as Bhūṣāvatī and others create desired ornaments made of gold and inlaid with jewels. In the seventh row, friends such as Annapūrṇā and others cook various food-based delicacies.

They cook various kinds of cooked foods, ever-new at every moment; others prepare diverse varieties of savory juices. In the eighth row, friends such as Sugandhavatī and others prepare various fragrances; friends such as Gānavatī and others sing; and friends such as Tantuvādinī and others perform beautiful singing to the accompaniment of rhythmic clapping.

In the ninth row, the friends such as Vilāsasurataraṅgavatī and Suratanandā, who are experts in the arts of fresh *kalās*, various types of seating, music, and literature—these friends, who embody the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas—perform the enumeration of His multitude of qualities through various types of hymns. In the eleventh row, Raṅgavatī and others cause [the Lord] to hear various wonderful, humble words filled with the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and moods (*bhāva*) of the stage, which are capable of generating love. In the twelfth row, there is the diverse movement of the friends.

Within that row, four rows shine forth in the inner portion. There, hundreds of houses, inlaid with gold and jewels, are brilliantly radiant. Along the jeweled avenues, rows of golden jasmine are exceedingly fragrant, and rows of pearl jasmine are most resplendent.

They exist there. Among them, the tree blossoms consist of various colors, are rich in fragrance, and shine manifoldly. Upon it, green, yellow, reddish, and red creepers remain, shining exceedingly with many varieties of beauty. The jewel-creepers shine intensely with internal jewel-blossoms. Within those creepers, subtle flowering creepers remain, shining brilliantly.

In those rows, the places of sport for her friends are most carefully maintained, rich with the fragrance of their virtues, and exceedingly endowed with representations of their forms. That row is extremely dear to Śrī Rādhā; whenever the desire to wander in the garden arises, Śrī Rādhā herself gathers [the flowers] therein and weaves the flower-garlands herself, while Rasikānanda gathers the flowers.

With her own hands, she fastens a string of necklaces woven from clusters of green, yellow, white, and red flowers around Śrī Rādhā’s neck; she shines most brilliantly. In that row, there is one palace—a secret place of play—that is filled with great splendor, made of jewels, seven-storied, and resplendent. One floor is made of gold; above that, the floor is adorned with jeweled staircases and inlaid with reddish-pink gems.

The series of stairs, their interiors dyed with many colors, becomes resplendent. Above that, the ground is exceedingly rich in beauty, fashioned from topaz (*puṣparāga*). There, the series of stairs shines forth; above that, the series of stairs is inlaid with strings of jewels, well-arranged in various hues, adorned with Jāmbūnada gold, and mutually permeated by fragrances. A well-fashioned jeweled creeper creates an exceedingly beautiful perimeter with the pollen of its flowers.

Above that, fashioned from moonstones, is the fourth level, which comes into contact with sprays of water. In a lotus pond filled with fragrant waters consisting of droplets from water-machines, Śrī Rādhikā and Śrī Rasikānanda experience the bliss of amorous union during the summer season and other times. Where they sit experiencing that bliss, there are coral swings entwined with jeweled creepers.

Upon a swing inlaid with jewels, the moonlight of the gems becomes even more intensely manifest through its reflections. Above that, a series of steps strung with jewels is formed. Above that, the ground, shimmering and sprinkled with the essence of fragrant gems, remains resplendent. Upon that ground, [the forms of] the sun, the moon, and fire—

The deities, assuming the form of female companions through their *ādhidaivika* (divine) aspect, attend upon her; on that ground, they experience the bliss of the joy of amorous union. Śrī Rādhikā’s companions, who were born from her own body along with Rasikānanda, are Kalāvatī, Sotsāhā, Premasaṃvalitā, Lajjāvatī, Guṇavatī, and Guṇāḍhyā. Furthermore, many other companions experience the pleasure of love and become filled with ecstatic emotion (*bhāva*).

Above that, a succession of staircases stands in the courtyard. This succession of staircases, which facilitates movement along a path of extreme bliss, is adorned with strings of jewels. Many levels, resonating with the attainment of the pleasure of delight, are joined together. Such is the mandala, endowed with twelve doors. At each of the twelve doors, there are twelve pathways for movement; thus, there is a successive movement along these pathways. That very mandala is renowned for its six qualities.

The six qualities serve as the six seasons while attending upon him. In this mandala, from the east, the Sun remains attending upon him, having assumed the form of a friend with his most gentle rays. From the north of that mandala, the Moon attends upon him. From the west of this mandala, Fire attends upon him in his transcendent (ādhidaivika) form. The planets, those stars, and other constellations always attend upon him, having assumed their transcendent forms.

Even Indra, assuming the form of a female companion, sits upon rows of celestial chariots together with divine damsels and constantly serves him. Even the Grandfather (Brahmā), assuming a subtle form, remains in the intermediate space, desiring to behold that world incessantly. Other guardians of the quarters, being perfected beings, constantly serve that sphere in their spiritual forms and remain immersed in the bliss of the worlds of that sphere. Devotees who worship that sphere should not resort to any other.

Those attached to other dharmas do not know this maṇḍala. That Lakṣmī spoke again: "What kind of action do those perform who worship the maṇḍala? He said: "They become worshippers of nothing else; they become self-natures perfected through the worship of nothing else. As self-natures, they worship the maṇḍala. The state of being both self and non-self arises. Completely immersed in the bliss of the Self, they do not contemplate any other flavor. Immersed in the bliss of the Self, they do not touch those who are not devotees. In the bliss of the Self..."

Their physical forms become magnificent; they do not listen to others, nor do they bow down to others, nor do they sing for others. Those devotees, permeated by the savor of the Self, hear bliss through the cultivation of the savor of delight in the Self and sing of that bliss. Filled with bliss and immersed in supreme rapture, the devotees chant the qualities [of the Lord]. Immersed in supreme rapture, they partake of His remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*); they never consume what is not a remnant. The devotees who worship His circle (*maṇḍala*) do not touch those who are not devotees.

Those other devotees who worship [other deities] are dependent on Ānanda, being inert in action; they are merely worshippers of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*). Those Brahmins who worship the sacrificial fire are merely worshippers of Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*). A worshipper of this circle should not even by mistake engage in conversation with them. Only those who are free from other religious duties and free from attachment to others attain this circle. It is only those free from other religious duties who attain it. Others do not know the Self by means of the Self. What is the use of saying more? By this very dharma [they are distinguished].

Those brāhmaṇas who are devotees of other sciences, who are dull-witted regarding action, who are devotees of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), who are devotees of Time (*kāla*), and who are indeed devotees of ritual acts, dharma, gods, and ancestors; those who are Śaivas, Śāktas, Kaulas, Jains, Pātañjalas, Mīmāṃsakas, Cārvākas who have fallen into dullness, and those firmly attached to other religions—they are such as these. But those who worship that Queen of Vraja together with Rasikānanda, they become experiencers of the essence of eternal bliss.

Those who are tender in the arts of love enumerate His multitude of qualities; they become those who sing of that very rasa; they become those who attain supreme delight. Those who hold a blade of *darbha* grass in their hands do not attain that rasa. Those who offer handfuls of sesame seeds to the ancestors do not reach that circle. Both gods and asuras are merely worshippers of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), whereas the gods who are worshippers of true knowledge (*sadvidyā*) are indeed Vaiṣṇavas; they, having transcended the gunas, worship the Mistress of Vṛndāvana.

They approach Him who is being served along with Rasikānanda. Immersed in His supreme qualities, they are constantly joined in experiencing the bliss of the joy of amorous union by night and by day. They come to experience the wonders of the arts of love. By virtue of His grace toward His devotees, the Lord Rasikānanda bestows His favor. Those who serve the Vraja-maṇḍala know that maṇḍala; knowing the maṇḍala, they practice devotion to the maṇḍala without attachment to anything else, always [for the sake of] all the world.

They become deeply attached to the *rasa-līlā*. Those who, through hundreds of mental longings, weave those pastimes day and night, become imbued with devotion within that circle and attain a steady mind. Upon hearing of that circle, they experience supreme bliss. Then Lakṣmī spoke this again to Nārāyaṇa: "O Ramā’s Beloved, he who indeed becomes absorbed in play in Vaikuṇṭha with exceeding love—this Nārāyaṇa immediately speaks his desired wish."

In the outermost Vraja-maṇḍala, there is a circle extending five yojanas. One who has entered that maṇḍala experiences exquisite delight. There, hundreds of houses made of gold and jewels exist, with thousands of rows and most magnificent galleries shining brilliantly. In those mansions, having ascended to the seven stories, men become immersed in the essence of pleasure and filled with ecstatic emotion. Men reside most excellently upon the jeweled floors.

There, the houses of the cowherds shine in beautiful rows. In every house of the cowherds, the eight great supernatural powers (*aṣṭamahāsiddhi*) are manifest. In every one of their homes, wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpadruma*) likewise flourish. Their domestic life exists solely for the sake of play; it is not for the sake of their own personal pleasure. Sometimes they engage in exceedingly intense play. For those who are truly perfected (*saṃsiddha*) are indeed immersed in such intense delight; thus these cowherds sing the glory of Rasikānanda.

Sporting with the Queen of Vraja, Māna-Rasikānanda follows many herds of cows that shine in green, yellow, white, bright, smoky, and coppery hues. Many herds, radiant in shades of tawny, black, white, and non-white, gleam in great numbers. Within these herds, in every row, hundreds of cows with udders like jars shine forth; the Queen of Vraja approaches them at every moment. Having cast a glance of compassion upon the cows, he remains nourishing them.

There is a circle of cows consisting of nectar, five *yojanas* in extent, possessing the luster of the perfected ones (*siddhas*). Herds of cows frolic there together with cowherds. There lies an ocean of milk; great bulls, accompanied by their calves and heifers, are sporting there. In various places, those cows, free from excrement and urine, enjoy the essence of nectar. Here and there, those cows frolic in grove after grove. Immersed in supreme delight, the cows are intent on play.
Surrounding the house of Nanda, herds of cows shine forth by the millions.

They all become gopīs, intent on the act of churning curd, singing various pastimes and sports together with Rasikānanda, the Queen of Vraja. That Lakṣmī spoke this again: "What austerity was performed by Kāmadhuk? How did such exceedingly great love arise? By her very milk, curd, fresh butter, essence of cream, and clarified butter, those [gopīs] are served by the Goddess of the Grove and manifested in the house of Vṛṣabhānu."

In that house, a person indeed engaged in amorous play with the Goddess of the Grove. In that house, herds of cows by the hundreds were resplendent. What did they do? What had they performed? What desires did they attain? How did they dwell in the joy of pleasure? What did they hear as they attained it? He, Nārāyaṇa, said: "There are only two types of cows: those who are perfected by nature (*saṃsiddhāḥ*) and those who are perfected through practice (*sādhanasiddhāḥ*)."

Those cows that stand within the circle of the cow-pen become fully perfected. On one occasion, I mentally entered that circle of the cow-pen where that Queen of Vraja was united with Rasikānanda. At that very moment, Kāmadhuk, who had been performing austerities, arrived in Vaikuṇṭha. Seeing me constantly delighting in a state of meditative absorption, Kāmadhuk reflected:

"Aha! This Nārāyaṇa, though eternally the beloved of Lakṣmī, is at every moment deeply absorbed in meditation upon someone—someone whom Nārāyaṇa himself, together with the Goddess, meditated upon later; someone whose portions of incarnations all the learned rely upon for their livelihood. If such is Nārāyaṇa, full of bliss and complete with all happiness and prosperity, upon whose meditation has he entered? Having thus understood her heart's desire, I spoke as follows:

"O wish-fulfilling cow, what has come upon your mind? She replied as follows: "Salutations to the infinite and great Kṛṣṇa, whose intellect is unimpeded; to the Lord of Yoga, to Yoga itself, and to Brahman of infinite power. Favored by you, devotees consider themselves to be absorbed in Him and thus become one with His nature. Herds of cows shine forth by the hundreds, and these cows are known as the essence of nectar. At that time, in the forests, there are groves covered with grass and hundreds of water-reservoirs filled with exquisite flavor."

They sit there resplendent. In that place, as they converse, the grasses, water-lilies, and medicinal herbs engage in conversation with them. The exceedingly well-nourished cows, having settled in the cow-pen, become ready to yield for the giver milk-essence, ghee-essence, curd-essence, butter-essence, and other such substances that are pleasant to consume. Radiant white and brindled cows, infused with essence, repeatedly approach the shining pens. Those cowherd girls sing along to the sound of churning the curds.

He experienced the pleasure of amorous love with them. Kāmadughā, who had come from Goloka, became one with that state upon merely hearing it from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, having chanted the mantra on her head at Govardhana Hill. That Queen of Vraja, Rasikānandā, manifested herself visibly. Being pleased, she granted him that divine play (līlā). Nārāyaṇa spoke this reply:

Oh, beloved! When the story of this world is heard, it settles into the hearts of all and destroys the latent tendencies of lust, anger, and the like. Exquisite devotion arises, and the delight of Rasikānanda is attained. The duties of one's own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) no longer act as obstacles. [She] performed austerities upon the peak of Govardhana Hill by the Govinda-puṣkariṇī lake. She chanted this great mantra. Listen to the meditation (*dhyāna*) for that mantra: *Oṃ namaḥ śrī-rādhā-rasikānandābhyām*. (Om, obeisances unto Śrī Rādhā and Rasikānanda.)

This is the root mantra. Whoever meditates upon it, conjoined with the twelve syllables and the seed-syllable *oṃ*, attains that very divine play (*līlā*). For this reason, a grove was established at Puṣkariṇī, renowned by the name Govindakuṇḍa. On that mountain on earth, she consumed the forest fruits, grass, and medicinal herbs. That wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadughā*), performing penance, wandered about that mountain. In this manner, she practiced penance for a hundred years.

On that Govardhana mountain, the jewel- and mineral-lattices and medicinal herbs are perpetually in bloom, laden with fruit, infused with essence, and exceedingly beautiful; there, numerous caves composed of jewels and gold shine as places for divine play. There, medicinal plants variegated with many colors, fashioned in various hues, are illuminated by their fruits and flowers. There, the Queen of Vraja performs most intense sports together with Rasikānanda.
Where groups of her friends were intent on recreation, there in that lotus pond, the Queen of Vraja revealed her own form—the form of Rasikānanda.

He exists as the very embodiment of rasa, manifest in this way, endowed with such exceeding qualities. He displayed his sport with his newly-wed bride. She, the cow of plenty, offered this hymn of praise: "Obeisance to the one whose essence is rasa; obeisance to the one whose essence is knowledge; obeisance to the one who eternally sports in the forest; obeisance to the cause of destroying the suffering inherent in the karma of one's own devotees; obeisance to the one who assumes a manifest bodily form; obeisance to the one whose essence is sporting amidst the waves of the Yamunā’s waters; obeisance to the one whose essence is the curiosity of amorous play; obeisance to the beloved of Kāma."

Salutations to the Self of desire! Salutations to the giver of a body permeated by desire! Salutations to the Original Creator! Salutations to the giver of the supreme cause of the beginning! Salutations to the Self whose body is attained through meditation on Śrī Rādhā! Salutations to the Self of aesthetic rasa! Salutations to the one whose form is the giver of a body fully intoxicated with rasa! Salutations to the one who sports in the inexpressible! Salutations to the giver of delight! Salutations to the Self who delights in the arts and pastimes of amorous play! Salutations to the giver of the delight of devotion! Salutations to the giver of the liberation of knowledge! Salutations to the one whose very nature is bliss! Salutations to the Seer of that!

Salutations to Him who is the cause; salutations to the one whose nature is sporting in the knowledge of the arts of love; salutations to the one beyond qualities (*aguṇa*); salutations to the giver of the quality of the form of creation; salutations to the enjoyer of the bliss of the pleasure of sporting with the *guṇas*; salutations to the giver of enjoyment; salutations to the one whose self is enjoyment; salutations to the one whose form is the Self; salutations to the giver of the essence of the form of the bliss of sexual union; salutations to the giver of infinite deeds; salutations to the one whose nature is the play of the sequence [of time]; salutations to the one whose form is Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa; salutations to the one whose form is Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Rādhā.

Salutations to the one who assumes many abodes and bodies; salutations to the one whose form consists of hundreds, thousands, millions, and tens of millions of abodes; salutations to the giver of delightful happiness at every moment; salutations to the soul who sports with numerous companions such as Viśākhā within the forest groves; salutations to the one whose nature is perfected devotion, beginningless and without origin; salutations to the giver of the virtue of charity; salutations to the embodiment of bliss; salutations to the one manifested for the sake of Vraja; salutations to the one whose nature is ultimate giving; salutations to the one who always wanders through the rows of Vṛndāvana.

"Obeisance to the one whose self is the twelve forests beginning with Ādi; obeisance to Him who may know the many beautiful forms that exist upon the earth. Obeisance again and again to the giver of delight in virtue, who possesses many forms such as Lakṣmī, Modesty, Fortitude, and Beauty. Having thus praised and stood before the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), who was overwhelmed by the great festival of seeing her, Rasikānanda, together with the goddess of the bower (Nikuñjadevī), said this to her: "Aho! Who are you that utter this praise? Devotion to me is difficult to attain in this world;
choose a boon even more difficult to obtain. [For] in your mind, my..."

Nothing remains superior to the sight [of you]. He who always praises you with devotion through hymns of praise attains his eternal desire. Again she said this: "O Lord, if a boon is to be granted, let me dwell in your world; may I serve you with the essence of cow's milk, curd, fresh milk, cream, butter, clarified butter, and thickened decoctions. Rasikānanda said: "By manifesting yourself in manifold ways, you shall always dwell as my beloved in the world; I shall protect you."

Dwell as you desire in this forest retreat. For those devotees of mine who have no other refuge, the duties of caste and stage of life do not arise as intermediate obstacles for them. No ritual actions arise as intermediate obstacles for them. No means of practice arises as an intermediate obstacle for them. Vows, sacrifices, Vedic hymns, and even the fruits of security and acquisition—whatever duties there may be that serve as means for dharma—all such things do not arise as intermediate obstacles for them.

There is a saying that the company of those Brahmins who accomplish ritual actions and knowledge, as well as those who accomplish the rituals of the scriptures of astrology, must be abandoned by force. The circumference of Vraja extends for ten yojanas. There, the cattle, birds, wild animals, cows, and other trees remain intent on nothing else; immersed in supreme rasa, they sing. Within that circle, even the gods are filled with a longing merely to behold it.

Those devotees who, engaging in the practice of devotion, go to that maṇḍala—the place of forest pastimes—and desire to dwell in Vraja, they alone become transcendent of all dharmas; they become transcendent of karma; they become transcendent of worldly attachment.
