They become worshippers of the Vraja-maṇḍala. Oh, Lakṣmī! That creation stands as something transcendent even of creation itself. One who is born from that creation becomes one who has taken refuge in the path of rasa.

If the mind is full of enthusiasm for this circle, then having attained acceptance therein, one remains absorbed in that state, experiencing its flavor with the delusion of the mind completely stilled. Whenever the gods, the ancestors, and Time strive toward the accomplishment of the journey, one becomes a student of the thousand branches of the Veda; yet, even while performing all sacrificial rites, one does not know that circle even in a dream.

Those wise ones who awaken others to Brahman and those ascetic yogis do not know that circle even in their dreams. Lakṣmī spoke again: "We recognize those devotees by certain signs. He said: "They always follow the path of love; they are neither despondent nor excessively attached to home, sense-objects, and the like."

They are not overly attached; they simply enjoy whatever objects come to them by chance. For the devotees, there is neither world-weariness, nor ascetic discipline, nor ritual action, but rather the service of spontaneous discourse and exclusive love—this is devotion (*bhakti*). Thus, one becomes naturally perfected, transcending such worldly existence. Then, they attain that divine play (*līlā*). In this way, the worshippers, having entered that circle, attain a state of being intensely united. That Lakṣmī spoke again as follows:

The devotees belonging to the path of rasa have attained that maṇḍala. This is their eleventh state. What is their destiny? He said: The devotees born in that maṇḍala possess the quality of self-delight; they are rich in the quality of delight, enriched by the non-dual path, and have attained those divine pastimes. Their bodies are marked with His name, their limbs are adorned with tulasī wood, and their forms are beautifully decorated with their own names. They remain engaged while entering into the meditative state of contemplating the Rāsa dance and other such pastimes.

In every bower, in every grove, and in every row, they attain a state of being fit for divine delight. They remain constantly relishing that very same discourse as if it were ever-new. Whether one is an outcaste, a Brahmin, or of another caste, whoever comes into the company of the devotees attains that very same divine play (*līlā*). If one has attained delight, they may occasionally perceive even the remnants of their food as the remains of [the Lord's] meal. Their perception of the water from those remnants is always that of a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*).

In that regard, a direct understanding arises from discourse concerning it. For those who worship that maṇḍala, what is their dharma? What is their action? What is their supreme essence? Do those who worship that maṇḍala possess the religious observances, vows, sacrifices, and duties of the various sacred fords? What might be their obstacle? Their primary concern becomes this: those who are rich in qualities, whose form is rasa, and who are immersed in the essence of bliss, become partakers of those very qualities.

This world, having attained the path of those [devotees] alone, shall forever be filled with birds. For those who are immersed in the bliss of the Self (Ātmānanda) at night and remain constantly absorbed in meditation during the day, the grace of the Goddess of the Grove (Nikuñjadevī) is eternally bestowed upon them. Those who are intensely attached to the Great Divine Play (Mahālīlā) never experience fear of the law of time (death); thus, their state of having achieved their life's purpose arises immediately. Even one of low caste attains the status of being of noble birth. Those who do not [possess these qualities] fall into evil destinies.

Those who worship the Vraja-maṇḍala dwell in Vraja; those who worship the Rāsa-maṇḍala attain the Rāsa-līlā and enjoy infinite bliss. Yaśodā and others, worshipping the Līlā and taking refuge in devotion, become united with the bliss of devotion. Nanda and others, worshipping the state of being supreme friends and attaining intimate union, reach the assembly of friends in the bliss of amorous play. Those who meditate upon the Goddess of the Grove (Nikuñjadevī) and worship the bliss of amorous play attain that very Līlā.

Those who have attained the ultimate bliss of divine love (*suratānanda*) and, being about to unite, take their place in the center of the circle of Vraja, attain the great pastimes (*mahālīlā*) and obtain the happiness of union. He said to Lakṣmī: "Those cowherds who have heard the highest limit [of that bliss] and attained the state of being friends (*sakhībhāva*) attain those very pastimes."

He who, having renounced all dharmas, becomes a worshiper of that maṇḍala, attains that very *līlā*; transcending all vows, transcending [ordinary] knowledge, shaken free from injunctions and prohibitions, duties and non-duties, virtues and vices, and existence and non-existence, he is constantly drawn into the *līlā* and, entering it, becomes intensely united with its aesthetic relish (*rasa*). Oh, Lakṣmī! This sixfold *rāsa-māyā* has been described; they become those who have attained that station by renouncing the entire *līlā*. That Lakṣmī spoke this again:

What is the nature of the place of the *rāsa*? Describe that place which its constant worshippers attain through mere devotion, by which they obtain that divine play (*līlā*). Nārāyaṇa replied: "It is one [place] resembling a thousand suns, consisting of supreme bliss. From it I, Brahmā, Rudra, the gods, and the guardians of the quarters are born; and by its power, numerous perfected devotees (*siddhas*) who have accomplished their spiritual means reside in that place. There, jewels bestow splendors in a super-divine form."

In that place, the perfected Sun, having assumed the form of a companion, attends upon [the Lord]; the Moon, having assumed an exceedingly subtle form, attends upon Him by his own self; and Fire, having assumed the form of a companion, remains attending upon Him. In that station, the gods always remain as perfected beings, constantly attending upon Him. On earth, the sun, moon, stars, and all others who provide assistance for spiritual practice, remain there only as attendants.
However, I shall describe that world from which these various beings arise; for there exist exceedingly many millions of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) undergoing an extraordinary manifestation.

In the center of that place, the light of the enclosure (āvaraṇa-jyotis) resides. Within the enclosure, which is a thousand yojanas in circumference, the multitude of the virtues of Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa are sung for the purpose of enumerating their qualities. At the first circumference, herds of cows are solely intent on play with the cowherds and cowherd girls. These places of play consist of grass, water, herbs, creepers, fruits, flowers, leaves, and tender shoots. Flavors such as honey, ghee, milk, yogurt, and fresh butter are exceedingly well-prepared there.

There, foods exist consisting of various combinations of many cooked juices—eatables, drinks, chews, and linctuses. There, trees pour down streams of nectar and honey for those who have approached them. There, lotus ponds are filled with nectar; having drunk that nectar there, one is utterly free from old age, death, birth from a womb, and destruction. There is a lake named Amṛtoda, which is drunk by the gods and is exceedingly filled with the nectar of the vision of that Goddess of the Grove.

In that place, groups of cowherds and cowherdesses, resting upon the sandy banks, are ever intent on play. On the second perimeter are groves, pleasure grounds, and trees bowed down with ripe fruits and flowers, as well as streams bent low with their foliage. Groups of cowherdesses devoted to play, through the divine immersion (*svāveśa*) of Śrī Rādhā—the goddess of the forest bower (*nikuñjadevī*)—become absorbed in play and are being gratified by the bliss of amorous union (*suratānanda*). There, the devotees remain intent on her play, absorbed in meditation upon her, and become one with her form.

In that place dwells the association of those devotees who are always seekers of the path of rasa. Oh! Experiencing that association, one becomes the very embodiment of the bliss of the connoisseur (rasika), permeated by the essence of the path of devotion. That alone is dharma; that alone is karma; that alone is knowledge (vidyā). Those which are dharmas are non-dharmas; those which are karmas are non-karmas. The third enclosure is the site of the Great Play (mahā-krīḍā-sthāna). In that place, seventy-one crores of forest groves (nikuñjas) shine resplendently.

Within which enclosure millions of pleasure-grounds shine resplendently; in which place there are fragrant circles of jewels that gleam brilliantly. Interspersed here and there are creepers of ruby gems entwined with blossoms of sapphire stones. Coral-formed peaks of gold, entwined as creepers upon golden grounds, make those pleasure-grounds exceedingly beautiful. This bliss of pleasure is ever-present for the devotees.

It is a source of happiness; by the mere hearing of its descriptions, all castes and all dharmas appear most clearly to everyone. Within that enclosure, it is the eternal playground of the mistress Śrī Rādhā and Śrī Rasikānanda. As the jeweled creepers sway, flocks of swans—yellow-necked, with red beaks and mouths—shine forth with extreme joy.

As if signaled by their melodious voices, they become like sweet-voiced cuckoos performing the chanting of the *sāman* hymns. Within that enclosure, upon the creepers, there are flocks of parrots that are intensely green with red beaks and yellow tails and wings; by them, the *Gāndharva-veda* is sung on every branch. In that enclosure, the female friends (*sakhīs*) born from the very limbs of Śrī Rādhikā are engaged in play.

Full of enthusiasm, longing, affectionate glances, and laughter; endowed with the quality of side-long glances, full of tender love, yet appearing soiled; possessing bedding and requisites, adorned with flowers, fearless, and shameless; yearning for sexual union, blissful in sexual union, wearing garlands, weary from pleasure, possessed of arts, skilled in the arts, discerning of qualities, steeped in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), permeated by desire, animated by emotion, alternating between sleep and wakefulness, and full of flavorful joy—by such names as these, various female companions experience the erotic sentiment of love.

Constantly devoted to play within the groves, those friends serve Rasikānanda. Within the creepers they prepare various foods and snacks, betel and other luxuries, and amidst the essence of amorous pastimes, they engage in games of pleasurable enjoyment. Having attained perfection through spiritual practice, the hosts of these friends and the flocks of birds have obtained this divine sport. Those perfected by their own means remain intent on play within that enclosure. Lakṣmī spoke as follows:

"By what means does this state come within the range of vision? He replied: "In the process of creation, there are three yogas: the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga), the yoga of action (karmayoga), and the yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga). Among these three yogas, the yoga of love (premāyoga) is far superior. Only those who possess the perfection of love experience the bliss of the joy of union."

That state is not attained through dharma, nor by sacrifices and charitable works (*iṣṭāpūrta*), nor by caste, nor by stage of life (*āśrama*), nor by sacred fords (*tīrtha*), nor by vows, nor by the yoga of emaciating the body, nor by action prescribed in the Vedas, nor by the means of investigating dharma and adharma. It belongs to him who is continuously absorbed in meditation upon That within the mind; wherever he may be situated, it is his.

In every place, we recognize that very Dharma; we recognize that very bliss. Its loss is an obstacle; that alone is true happiness which consists in passing the time in conversation with His devotees and in discourse regarding the pastimes of His concealment. O Lakṣmī, those for whom even the mere objects acquired during household festivals are dedicated to Him attain that world. Oh, this creation is indeed of the nature of aesthetic rasa!

For them, dharmas other than the path of rasa become increasingly obstructive. Having brought about the gathering of the mind and fixed the senses within the mind through mental disposition (*bhāva*), they attain absorption day and night. In whatever obscuration the mind becomes immersed, one who follows that path, favored by that Goddess of the Grove (*nikuñjadevī*), comes to serve her world, whether by night or by day, at the proper time or otherwise.

"Aha! Though the functioning of your mind is exceedingly fickle, your devotees are free from attachment to worldly existence; they are desireless in this world, absorbed in You, indifferent, complete in heart, and profoundly peaceful. They possess equal vision, being free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, free from the pairs of opposites, and free from possessions. Among them, O highly fortunate one, are those who, devoid of any other path, behold themselves as absorbed in You and thus serve the Self."

For those who are followers of that path and are ever-venerating devotees, there arises an expectation for the pinnacle of the characteristic of divine love. Oh, how wonderful is the fourth enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), the great abode! Within this enclosure is the personal dwelling place of the Mistress herself. There are hundreds of thousands of groves and bowers, covered with creepers, golden-hued, coral-colored, stainless, pure, manifest pearl-strings, and radiant; here resides the movement of these female companions (*sakhīs*). Between the subtle creepers are the furnishings for the bed.

Amidst many creepers, the *rāsa* pastime occurs most intensely. This *rāsa* is naturally integrated [with the divine essence]. Within that enclosure, having assumed forms intent on supreme play, the Queen of Vraja experiences the bliss of the *rāsa-līlā*, sporting together with Rasikānanda. The fifth enclosure is composed of light. There, nectar-filled medicinal herbs shine forth, endowed with fruits and flowers, and possessed of the juice of ripened fruit.
The food-flavors, being well-cooked, savory, and endowed with the desired tastes of pungent, bitter, and sweet, were enjoyed by Śrī Rādhikā in many places and partaken of by Rasikānanda.

They become resplendent. Through the manifestation of the Self, manifold happiness arises. The place of enjoyment becomes exceedingly magnificent. In various locations within that enclosure, the pleasure of delight increases greatly. The sixth enclosure consists of light; therein, palaces made of gold shine brilliantly. A hundred luminous palaces gleam there. Caskets adorned with gold and inlaid with gems, as well as those encrusted with gold, appear most beautiful.

There, ornaments studded with gold and jewels shine resplendently, as do garments most appropriate to each. In that seventh enclosure, the place of dalliance, groups of female companions such as Śṛṅgāravatī and others appear radiant; having divided themselves into a hundred forms, they enjoy the pleasure of amorous delight through manifold sensual delights. This seventh enclosure, the place of play, extends for a thousand yojanas.

On every side, the jeweled pillars are exceedingly rich in flavor and abundant in fragrance. The ground, enriched with the quality of supreme flavor, soft and fragrant as gold, becomes intensely filled with bliss as if it were about to be enjoyed. There, the movements of the creepers consist of nothing but the movement from the higher to the lower. By the moonlight of the jewels set in gold, every single object is reflected.

There, Kalāvatī, Gānavatī, Sugandhā, Nṛtyaparā, Viśadā, Bhogaparā, Bhogavatī, Bhogābhijñā, Ratikalābhijñā, Kāmasukhā, Kāmāturā, Niḥśaṅkā, Sadānandā, Suratasukhā, Suratānandā, Suratamagnā, Āsanabhedābhijñā, Atirasadānābhijñā, Rasadā, and Rasadātṛbhogābhijñā—these companions are perfected (saṃsiddhā), while others are accomplished through practice (sādhanasiddhā) and are experts in many arts.

In that enclosure of the mandala, there was a great chamber provided with a bed and furnishings. Kalāvatī prepared the bedding and articles; she who is eager for amorous play bestowed the longing for amorous play; she who is shameless bestowed fearless happiness; she who emerges through amorous passion bestowed the blissful taste of love’s intensity through embracing, kissing, and bowing; Rativatī bestowed the pleasure of sexual union; and Ratikallolā, her eyes half-closed in languor from the intensity of the flavor of passion, bestowed the joy of dalliance.
Rasikānanda remains there, experiencing happiness with the Queen who has gone to her private bower-house; in that bower, a well-prepared companion provides the comfort of a bed in every corner.

A certain female swan, always situated in the midst of her circle of friends within that enclosure, constantly intent on play, approaches while sporting with Śrī Rādhā and Rasikānanda through the sound of her call. At that time, she sings to them with a sweet-voiced throat in such a way that it becomes a subtle melody. During the pastime of the lover’s quarrel, at the word of Rasikānanda, she propitiates the Queen of Vraja and continuously bestows upon her supreme enthusiasm.

That Queen of Vraja becomes all the more like a kalahamsī (swan-maiden) as she approaches him; that kalahamsī, experiencing supreme bliss due to her being exceedingly dear to Rasikānanda, is most pleasing. She is ever awake, she is ever a knower of virtues, and she is ever a knower of the enjoyment of the rasa of amorous union. That kalahamsī captivates the minds of all her companions with her own play; that kalahamsī becomes exceedingly beloved to Rasikānanda.

"That Kalahaṃsī was indeed perfected through spiritual practice. Lakṣmī spoke again: "Aho! By what practice did Kalahaṃsī previously attain this place? She attained a great station! It is most wonderful! By what constant practice does she become the intimate play-companion of Śrī Rādhā? This Nārāyaṇa replied: "That Kalahaṃsī is Sarasvatī, the daughter of Brahmā at the beginning of creation; from her all kinds of powers originate."

The four Vedas, the Upavedas, the Purāṇas, and the Dharmaśāstras—all those that exist or will exist upon the earth—arose from her. That daughter of Brahmā remained even as she reached the prime of youth. On one occasion, she came to my world and performed service unto me; for her own happiness, she became absorbed in meditation upon me. Serving me for a long time, I was pleased by her devotion and showed her Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of my divine play.

In that realm, the places where you and I have played shine forth with splendor. There in Vaikuṇṭha, numerous devotees—such as Jayanta, Kumuda, Jaya, Vijaya, Garuḍa, and others—dwell as hundreds of radiant attendants (*pārṣadas*). There, the fourfold liberations (*muktis*) abide, being served; there, forests exist by the millions in great abundance. Sā Vāgdevī, her mind filled with intense longing and her heart completely immersed in bliss, attained happiness through my glance of grace and prayed for the Great Pastimes (*mahālīlā*).
Then she was addressed by me:

"O Goddess of Speech, go to your dwelling in Vraja. On this earth, there is a lake named Acchoda in Kāmavana, upon the Sugandha stone. Having bathed there in Acchoda and meditated upon the Queen of Vraja on the Sugandha stone, attain union with Rasikānanda. In that place, love arises through the state of identifying with the Self of all. Experiencing the bliss of divine love, the devotees become fit for His pastimes.

Constantly attending upon Vṛndāvana, the Forest of Desire, and Śrī Govardhana, she arrived at the Apsaras Puṣkariṇī in Acchoda, where she remained immersed for a long time. She spent a hundred years serving the pastimes of Vraja. On a single Kārttikī full moon, the residents there perform the Rāsa-līlā; many among the assembly of devotees, having assumed the forms of Kalahaṃsīs (female swans), displayed that divine play.

By night and by day, that Queen of Vraja became exceedingly visible to Rasikānanda’s sight. Seeing her—who was of the nature of supreme bliss, situated in the midst of a multitude of friends, intent on great play, and possessing a most enchanting form—he became filled with emotion through a love that purifies the senses. Becoming gracious, she, who was exceedingly tender and beautiful, said, "Choose a boon. He replied: "If a boon is to be granted, then may I always be a companion to you during your great pastimes; what need is there for any other boon?"

This was indeed the heart's desire regarding the sport that was seen. Having been told "So be it" by those two, she went to her own place. From that day forward, she became even more intent on play. In every bower and thicket, merging branch by branch with him in the form of a *kalahaṃsī* (female swan), she praised him with the singing of the *Sāmans* and with her inner devotion, performing various wonderful sports. She reached the great place of delight and remained immersed in the great divine play, experiencing the bliss of *rati*.

That female swan, having left her own flock, once at a certain time during the latter part of the night, sang of the dalliance arising from amorous union. At other times, she would sing of the sport of bathing. In the dalliance of love, she became exceedingly manifest with the arising of ever-new passion at every moment. As she sang of these dalliances, she became as if about to engage in sexual union.

In the state of enjoyment, there are at every moment fresh coverings composed of garlands, sandalwood, betel, agallochum, musk, camphor, and saffron; and upon many beds, fragrant and ornate, hang beautiful sandalwood trees entwined with flowering creepers that embrace one another's lovely limbs.

The spaces between the creepers are exceedingly endowed with golden fragrance; therein, in the context of love, she becomes a place for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*) as she sings together. Her ornaments are fragrant gold; the gems set in gold become filled with excellent scent. She causes [her companions] to wear garments that are being permeated by an intense fragrance. Thus Kalahaṃsī offered praise with her words. She became exceedingly beloved for her singing by the Goddess of the bower.

This is the great sentiment of erotic love (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). Not following the paths of injunction or prohibition, she exists within her own being immediately after the erotic sentiment; she becomes immersed in that sentiment when addressed, and she exists in a state of passion. Through her own being, she extends this mimicry of the other; she projects the forest-play into her mind. Intensely longing for union, like a female swan (*kalahaṃsī*), she gives the desired fruit and honey from among the creepers to Rādhā during the night and day, and then attends to others.

Therein lies a single lotus pond, four yojanas in length, filled with the sweet essence of nectar. There, clusters of lotuses exist—golden, fragrant, exceedingly soft, and enchanting. In that lotus forest, a radiant kalahamsī (swan) dwells, intent on sporting and play. Oh, Lakṣmī! When, through the rising fortune of someone and by the grace of that goddess of the bower, the dharma of exclusive reliance [upon her] arises, then true delight (*rati*) manifests.

To that extent, the bodily limitations of karma—namely hunger, thirst, exhaustion, delusion, fear, and suffering—as well as pleasures, do not exist in the same manner as they do for the gods and others. Having understood that vows, fasts, dharma and adharma, ancestral rites and non-rites, whatever duties there may be, and other radiant duties consisting of various fasts and their resulting merits or demerits, he who becomes transcendent of all such dharmas attains that very maṇḍala; thus it is said: "Aha! One should practice meritorious conduct that is delightful; one's state of being should become exceedingly pure."

In the play of divine enjoyment (*saṃbhoga-līlā*), this world remains as the bliss of sexual union (*suratānanda*). Experiencing the happiness of the bliss of sexual union, devotees lead themselves to a state of identity with that [bliss]. Having abandoned both merit and demerit, they become equanimous and natural in disposition. Immersed in supreme rasa, they become endowed with knowledge, austerity, meditation, friendliness, the arts, and virtuous qualities. An atheist who possesses attachment to other [worldly] conceptions does not attain that world.

Oh Lakṣmī, perhaps by the dawning of great fortune, there exists a delight in this enclosure where the trees are bowed with fruit and immersed in the desired nectar-like essence of flowers; where the branches are bent with blossoms. In the fifth [chapter].

Within the enclosure, flocks of parrots and mynas, fully perfected and resplendent, dwell together. Some mango trees, laden with ripe fruit, remain there constantly being enjoyed. There is one parrot, deeply immersed in rasa and perfected through spiritual practice (*sādhanasiddha*), who is exceedingly dear; the Mistress of Vraja herself cleanses his wings and beak with her own hand, and Rasikānanda also personally gives him food. He has a female companion, a maina, who is even more perfected in her practice.

That pair of parrots and mynas becomes exceedingly like companions in the play that delights the connoisseurs (*rasika*). Among them, the female myna is constantly intent upon the sport. On grounds of golden hue and encircled by jewels, there is a pleasure grove furnished with beds and requisites. There, the arboreal pathways are exceedingly rich in beauty. There, the parrots and mynas, having attained perfection through their practice, are devoted to play; they become intensely attached to the great sport.

"Aha! This path of aesthetic relish (*rasa-mārga*), though exceedingly difficult to attain, has become accessible. Aha! By virtue of great fortune and through the grace of that Goddess of the Grove (*nikuñja-devī*), it becomes most beloved. Love arises from love; devotion arises from devotion; and affection arises from affection—therefore, for one who has reached this state through the dawning of fortune, aha! all become fortunate, having fulfilled their purpose, and possessing all sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*). Immersed in supreme relish, enjoying it intensely, they experience ultimate bliss."

Those who enjoy this divine play (*līlā*) and those who are indeed devoted to this divine play—they are the devotees (*bhakta*). When the dawning of great fortune occurs to a superior degree, then there arises conviction in this divine play. They are the performers of dharma; they are the observers of vows. Those for whom there is a delight in worshiping the divine play, they become the observers of vows. [This applies to] him whose mind enters into the great divine play.

He who, having become weary of both ritual injunction and prohibition, becomes possessed of the state of mind regarding this divine play (*līlā*), he alone shall be fit for that play. This is the grace bestowed upon those who possess conviction. Lakṣmī spoke this again: "The mind becomes possessed of the state of being in the secret play; my own heart, overwhelmed by intense passion, has become possessed of that state."

Who is Śuka? Who is the female śārikā that has attained such a state of being? She, in whom Rasikānanda’s mind becomes permeated with extreme affection—that Vrajeśvarī showed him the utmost love. He has reached a station most difficult to attain; his course of delight is uninterrupted.

Their fitness for union was becoming even greater. He said, "This is Nārāyaṇa. Listen, Lakṣmī: in the beginning of creation, there was a Brāhmaṇa named Sumantu, born of the Kauśika lineage. He was born in the land of Kānyakubja and became exceedingly devoted [to the Lord]. His wife was Manoramā, who was deeply intent on the path of supreme devotion. That couple, being most fortunate and endowed with great affection, remained constantly engaged in service, their hearts intent on union."

Those two, husband and wife, their hearts possessed by excessive affection, remained serving that Queen of Vraja together with Rasikānanda from time to time. They became exceedingly attached to the forest pastimes. By what great surge of fortune and through the association of devotees did they reach the forest of Vṛndāvana? There, in that Vṛndāvana—a forest of desire—they arrived at the grove of Kadamba trees in Vṛṣabhānu-pura, at Nanda-grāma, by the purifying lake.

How long did the couple remain dwelling in such a secluded place for their amorous pastimes? The husband and wife became intensely attached to the forest with longing. Along with her heart's desire, the Queen of Vraja came within the range of Rasikānanda’s vision. Intent on play during the great pastime, they conversed and united. From that day forward, the couple remained devoted to the play of the great pastime. Lakṣmī spoke this secret.

"What is the nature of the creation of the residents of Vraja? What is the nature of those who are fully perfected (*saṃsiddha*)? Which other living beings were manifested at the beginning of creation? What is the form of the individual soul (*jīva*)? And what are bondage and liberation like? Again, this Nārāyaṇa spoke: "Aha! This phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is established from time immemorial (*anādi-saṃsiddha*). Just as Brahman is threefold in nature—consisting of existence (*sat*), consciousness (*cit*), and bliss (*ānanda*)—existence (*sat*) exists by virtue of its pervasiveness, and consciousness (*cit*) consists of light."

But the Supreme Person, consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), transcends [all]. Just as this world of Brahman-bliss becomes *saccidānanda* (being-consciousness-bliss), so too does the multitude of individual souls (*jīvasaṅgha*) become threefold. He said this: "What is this multitude of souls? What is their vision? What is their state? He replied this: "Listen. This soul is a portion of consciousness (*cidaṃśa*) that has been established from time immemorial. He said this: "If the soul is a portion of consciousness, how does it fall into insentience through ignorance (*ajñāna*)? He replied: "Just as this [soul] has been established from time immemorial..."

Likewise, the host of individual souls (*jīvasaṅgha*) and *māyā* are established as beginningless. That [māyā] exists pervading [all things] in three ways; thus, that very soul becomes threefold. He said this: "The host of individual souls exists in three ways. Describe them. He replied: "That which has the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*) consists of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). It performs various actions (*karma*). Castes (*varṇa*), stages of life (*āśrama*), duties (*dharma*), and means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) are joined together. Their origin and maintenance [belong to it]. The soul whose nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) becomes a knower (*jñānin*)."

He becomes one who follows the path beyond action (*niṣkarmamārgīya*). Those living beings (*jīva*) whose nature is bliss, by abandoning all *dharma*, remain as the very essence of the bliss of rasa, being served by the great divine play (*mahālīlā*). Neither *dharma* nor *adharma* obstruct them within that great play. He said this: "By what *māyā* is the living being joined so that he becomes devoted to the path of action? He replied: "The form of *māyā* is threefold. That form which is the form of existence (*sadrūpa*), when this multitude of living beings is permeated by it, they become devoted to the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*)."

The multitude of individual souls (*jīva-saṅgha*), conjoined with *māyā* in the form of consciousness (*cid-rūpā*), becomes renunciants (*saṃnyāsī*). Through *māyā* conjoined with bliss (*ānanda*), they become essentially composed of bliss. Indeed, the essence of bliss is the primary cause of the Great Divine Play (*mahā-līlā*). I shall describe their activities exactly as they are. Among them, those who follow the path of ritual action (*karma-mārgīya*), who teach ritual action, and who are demons (*asura*) lacking conviction in the Great Forest Play (*mahā-vana-līlā*), being inert in action (*karma-jaḍa*) and devoted to other [deities], do not find the other path because of those very limitations (*upādhi*).

Those who worship fire undergo birth within subtle bodies (liṅga-śarīra) consisting of the latent impressions (vāsanā) of sacrificial acts. Through that subtle body composed of latent impressions, they experience birth, maintenance, and dissolution. Therefore, this nature of the individual soul (jīva) consists of the subtle body.

When, having shaken off all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one’s mind enters into the Great Play (*mahālīlā*)—O Lakṣmī!—then, knowing and knowing that Play, meditating upon it, and utterly casting aside the pride and qualities of egoism, as well as desire, anger, greed, delusion, fear, pleasure, pain, shame, lack of shame, ignorance, infatuation, envy, and so forth, which are born of the body; and casting aside the various worldly states produced by many births—whether *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or *tāmasa*—along with the ever-shining merit and demerit, and those things dependent on scriptures, mantras, tantras, herbs, alchemy, astrology, and the play of speech, [one enters] the Great Play.

He would have entered [it]. He expands himself as being identical with that. When his mind has entered elsewhere into another object, then he reaches that *liṅga*. Śrī said this: "You have stated that the individual soul (*jīva*) is subject to *māyā*, by which the *jīva* [is bound] to the *liṅga* of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)."

It arises within the body. By what power does one become possessed of effort? He replied: "Therefore, through the dawning of great fortune, by chance, with the assistance of a guru, and through association with holy men who are free from other dharmas, the mind becomes cleansed of sin. Through absorption in that [mind], one shakes off the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) by that path and approaches the Queen of Vraja in her great pastimes, serving her together with Rasikānanda. Lakṣmī said this.

"What is the nature of the *jīva*? In what form does it undergo birth, existence, and dissolution? He replied: "This *jīva* is indefinable. Weapons do not cut it; fire does not burn it; the wind does not dry it; water does not moisten it. Whichever latent impression (*vāsanā*) it encounters, assuming that very subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*), it remains. The *jīva* is utterly bound by latent impressions."

Freed from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he is attached to the great play (*mahālīlā*); he is neither disgusted with nor excessively attached to *saṃsāra*. This group of living beings, having attained perfection, assumes various bodily states through the differentiation of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *māyā*. But the unperfected one remains conjoined with a body of attachment. He spoke this:

"What is the nature of the body? What are its qualities and what are its defects? By what is there bondage in the body? By what alone is there liberation in that body? Who is without attributes (*nirupādhi*)? What knowledge arises therein? By what kind of body is there bondage? By what kind does liberation occur? He replied: "The distinctions of bodies are twofold. The body itself is produced by karma, and it arises by chance through the grace of that Goddess Nikuñjadevī."

For those who are dull-witted by their karma, the self becomes dull-natured through the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by that karma. Those from whose grace [this] arises find delight in the path of affection (*sneha*). Those for whom there is delight in the path of liberation (*nirvāṇa*) become renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*). The body, moreover, consists of the eleven organs: the five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, and the mind (*manas*), which is born as having the nature of both. There are the five great elements (*mahābhūtas*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*), the three qualities (*guṇas*), and the twenty-fifth is the individual soul (*jīva*).

The twenty-sixth principle, Mahāviṣṇu, is the eternal witness. These individual souls (*jīvas*), experiencing the limiting adjunct of the body, undergo pleasure and pain. They possess qualities common to all bodies; they encounter and experience passion and the like, as well as desire, anger, greed, delusion, old age, death, happiness, and sorrow. This body, seized by decay, is like a city of the Gandharvas, consisting merely of mental constructs.

It happens thus: all those qualities, having departed from the emergence of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), shake off the subtle body and lead the Self to identity with That. Those defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth are conjoined with the body; when they are employed for that purpose [of liberation], they become the means (*sādhana*). He said this: "How can passion and the rest become the means, given that through their association one has fallen into a state of deficiency?"

"How is it that passion and the other afflictions, when employed for the sake of the Blessed One, attain the state of being free from karma? [The Lord] replied: "This desire, this anger, this greed, and this delusion impel the individual soul (jīva) for the sake of its own play. He said: 'Māyā is threefold. The qualities such as desire, anger, and so forth, produced by Māyā in its aspect of existence (sadrūpa), become the instigators of the arising of saṃsāra. When the souls (jīvas) take refuge in the aspect of consciousness (cidrūpa), they resort to those qualities and thereby fall into a state of insentience."

The individual souls (jīvas), having taken refuge in the nature of bliss (ānanda-rūpa), have attained identity with it. This essence consisting of bliss (ānandamaya-rasa), which is transmigratory, attains the Self through its own state of being composed of bliss. Attachment and other qualities such as desire and anger become the means [to this end]. Oh! This multitude of souls, entering the path of aesthetic essence (rasa-mārga), meditates upon the Self as identical with that essence; thereby shaking off the subtle body (liṅga) composed of latent impressions (vāsanā) and practicing the state of the Self, they attain identity with it.

As the Self dissolves each and every latent impression (*vāsanā*), so too does that respective *liṅga* dissolve through that very state. One who is intensely devoted to this path, having shaken off the *liṅga*, becomes free from evil and attains the state of pure being. This path which has been described to you is not known by the gods or others; it is not known by Rudra and the rest. By worshipping that mandala, one attains identity with it. This secret has been told; it must not be spoken by you to anyone.

Having meditated upon one's own beloved in the heart, one dissolves through that very state of being. "Oh, Lakṣmī! Devotees who have taken refuge in this path, having abandoned the attributes of the bodily adjuncts, attain the state of possessing those [divine] qualities"—thus do the chanters of the Sāman sing continuously in secret. "Whatever may be deficient in syllables or words, or lacking in prosodic measures—all that be forgiven, O Rādhā; be gracious, O Beloved of Hari. Thus ends the *Sāmarahasyopaniṣad*.
